        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"overview-6\"\u003e7.1 Overview\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThis section sets expectations for managing data as a strategic asset that supports better public services, evidence-based decisions, operational effectiveness and responsible innovation across government, including the safe and transparent use of artificial intelligence.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eEach organisation shall assign senior accountability for data, with clear ownership for data strategy, governance, quality, protection, ethical use, sharing and reuse (see 4.6.5).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should follow cross-government strategies, standards and governance for government digital and data, including guidance from the Data Standards Authority, the Government Data Quality Framework, the Data and AI Ethics Framework, the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard, and relevant security, privacy and technology standards (see section 4).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eData should be retained, archived or disposed of in accordance with the organisation’s retention schedule, information management policy, security requirements and legislation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: The National Data Library is the home of UK public data to inform decisions and build services. \u003csup id=\"fnref:5:1\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:5\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 5]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: Attention is drawn to:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) \u003csup id=\"fnref:17:1\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:17\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 17]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe Data Protection Act \u003csup id=\"fnref:18:1\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:18\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 18]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ePublic Records Act \u003csup id=\"fnref:19\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:19\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 19]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eFreedom of Information Act \u003csup id=\"fnref:20\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:20\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 20]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"data-management-principles\"\u003e7.2 Data management principles\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eData management must be lawful, ethical, secure, transparent and proportionate to the purpose for which data is collected, used, shared and retained.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should ensure their data is fit for purpose by:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eidentifying critical data assets, including those needed for service delivery, policy, operations, analysis, reporting, cross-government sharing and AI-enabled services\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eassigning accountable owners and stewards for critical data assets, with clear responsibilities for governance, quality, access, protection and lifecycle management\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emaintaining metadata and catalogues so that data can be found, understood, validated, reused and shared appropriately\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eputting processes in place to identify, prioritise, remediate and monitor data quality issues at source\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should ensure their data is trusted, accessible and reusable by:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebeing able to evidence that critical data assets meet minimum standards for governance, quality, security, privacy and ethical use, based on their purpose and context\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eensuring data is discoverable through maintained catalogues, with clear metadata, lineage, quality information and access conditions\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eapplying appropriate security, privacy, access and information assurance controls so data can be shared safely and lawfully\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should ensure their data architecture (see 7.4) supports interoperability, reuse and secure exchange by:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eidentifying authoritative sources for critical data and ensuring they are appropriately governed, maintained and provisioned\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eusing open standards, common data models and agreed reference data where appropriate to improve consistency and interoperability\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebeing able to evidence that Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), data exchange platforms and analytical environments meet appropriate standards for governance, security, privacy and control\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edocumenting classifications, sensitivity, criticality, retention requirements, lineage and usage restrictions so data is handled appropriately\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emaintaining integrated catalogues for data, interfaces, standards and data sharing arrangements\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eensuring data used to train, test, validate or operate AI systems is documented, lawful, representative, secure and appropriate for the intended use\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThere should be accountable ownership for data quality, protection, security, ethics, access, sharing and reuse, supported by cross-government guidance, frameworks and standards.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo support continuous improvement and help senior leaders prioritise investment, organisations should assess data maturity across technical, governance, cultural, skills and leadership factors using an appropriate framework.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThroughout the planning, implementation and evaluation of projects, programmes, services, analytical work and AI-enabled solutions, organisations should use the Data and AI Ethics Framework to ensure data and AI are used appropriately, responsibly and transparently. \u003csup id=\"fnref:21\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:21\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 21]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSee Government Functional Standard GovS 002: Project Delivery.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere specified, publication of data and analysis should be done through approved routes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor example, publication of official statistics should follow the protocols set out in the Code of Practice for Statistics, which provides the framework for trustworthy, high-quality and valuable statistics. These principles are relevant across data management and should be followed where appropriate. \u003csup id=\"fnref:22\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:22\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 22]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: The Data Standards Authority exists to improve how the public sector manages data, including by setting standards for sharing and using data across government. \u003csup id=\"fnref:23\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:23\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 23]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: The government’s Data and AI Ethics Framework guides appropriate and responsible use of data, data-driven technologies, automated decision-making and AI in government and the wider public sector.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eIt helps public servants identify ethical considerations, manage risks and maintain trust across the lifecycle of data and AI projects.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"data-frameworks-and-operating-models\"\u003e7.3 Data frameworks and operating models\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations shall follow appropriate guidance when implementing data frameworks and operating models, including for cross-government data sharing, business intelligence, artificial intelligence, machine learning, automation and advanced analytics.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: The following products provide best practice guidance:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ePrinciples for securing personal data in government services \u003csup id=\"fnref:24\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:24\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 24]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAI Playbook for UK Government \u003csup id=\"fnref:25\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:25\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 25]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eData and AI Ethics Framework \u003csup id=\"fnref:21:1\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:21\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 21]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eThe Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard \u003csup id=\"fnref:26\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:26\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 26]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"data-architecture\"\u003e7.4 Data architecture\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eData architecture describes the systems, processes, standards, models and structures used to acquire, create, move, store, query, protect, share, archive and dispose of data to meet user, service and business needs.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations need confidence that the right data is available when needed, in usable, accessible, secure and standardised formats, and that data and system capabilities meet user, service and operational needs.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhen developing data architecture proposals, organisations should follow relevant standards, guidance and tools, including open standards, API standards, security guidance, data protection requirements, AI assurance guidance and guidance on managing data assets (see 8.8).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: For practical advice, see the data management capability framework and the GOV.UK collection of design guidance for application programming interfaces. \u003csup id=\"fnref:27\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:27\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 27]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe following web-based API standards guidance will help your organisation deliver the best possible services to users:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eUK Government Reference Architecture for Data and APIs \u003csup id=\"fnref:28\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:28\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 28]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eGraphQL Guidance - an API specification originally developed by Facebook as an alternative to REST for querying complex data structures \u003csup id=\"fnref:29\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:29\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 29]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAPI Management Guidance - enabling you to standardise how teams design, launch and manage APIs in your organisation \u003csup id=\"fnref:30\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:30\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 30]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eDomain Guidance for api.gov.uk - contact the Government Digital Service to get a domain for your API on GOV.UK \u003csup id=\"fnref:31\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:31\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 31]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"managing-data-quality\"\u003e7.4.1  Managing data quality\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eData quality should be measured using dimensions such as completeness, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness, validity and accuracy. The dimensions and thresholds used should reflect the intended use, risk, sensitivity and impact of the data, including where data supports AI or automated decision-making.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should develop a culture of data quality, by:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etreating issues at source and committing to ongoing monitoring, reporting and continuous improvement\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etargeting improvements where they add the most value or reduce the greatest risk\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emanaging data quality proactively across the data lifecycle\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emaking data quality visible to users through metadata, quality statements or other appropriate information\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eA data quality action plan may be used to manage improvement work. If used, it should identify owners, priorities, root causes, actions, measures, timescales and reporting arrangements, and should be reflected in the organisation’s information and data plan (see 8.5).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should use measurable characteristics to improve data quality, and should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emaintain an assessment of the current level of data quality\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eset targets for appropriate quality levels in the future\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emonitor quality to ensure that planned improvements are made\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eSuch quality measures should ensure that accountability is clear (see 4.6.5) and that:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003equality characteristics are assessed in relation to a specific use at various points\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe impact of changes to relevant data collection, storage, and processing is assessed\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: The Data Quality Hub provides information and support on data quality. \u003csup id=\"fnref:32\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:32\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 32]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: Further information and guidance can be found in the Data Quality Framework. \u003csup id=\"fnref:33\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:33\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 33]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"data-and-information-asset-management\"\u003e7.5 Data and information asset management\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eData and information asset management enables an organisation to identify, record, understand, govern and maintain its data and information assets so it knows what it holds, where it is held, who is accountable for it, how it can be accessed, how it should be protected, and how it is retained, reused, shared or disposed of.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should follow existing standards and guidance, including the data asset management policy where applicable, and should manage data so that:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecritical data and information assets are identified, recorded, maintained and reported where required\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emetadata is actively managed to describe data and information assets, ownership, quality, lineage, sensitivity, retention, disposal and access conditions\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata is shared by default where lawful, ethical, secure and appropriate, and where there are no valid reasons not to share\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata is reused to maximise value and minimise unnecessary duplication, collection and storage\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edataset linkage is managed safely, with appropriate privacy, security and ethical controls\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eaccess permissions are strictly managed and reviewed regularly\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata governance, security, privacy and compliance requirements are observed throughout the data lifecycle\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einteroperable data infrastructure, open standards and integrated catalogues are used where appropriate\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edata assets used in AI systems are recorded with their purpose, provenance, quality, limitations, access conditions and retention requirements\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: For information asset ownership, see government guidance on the Information Asset Owner role. \u003csup id=\"fnref:34\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:34\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 34]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: The resources listed provide best practice for managing and supporting data asset management:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAPI Catalogue \u003csup id=\"fnref:35\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:35\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 35]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eReference Data for Use Across Government \u003csup id=\"fnref:36\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:36\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 36]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eAddress Base Guidance - use free property and street information to add geospatial data to your projects and comply with the UPRN standard \u003csup id=\"fnref:37\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:37\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 37]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"data-engineering\"\u003e7.6 Data engineering\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe purpose of data engineering is to make data useful, accessible, reliable and secure for authorised users so they can make informed decisions, improve services and optimise organisational performance.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eData engineering includes acquiring, ingesting, validating, transforming, modelling, documenting, storing, securing and provisioning data in formats that meet user needs and support safe reuse, including for analytics, automation and AI where appropriate.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eTo ensure useful and accessible data through data engineering, organisations should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003efollow cross-government data standards, open standards and agreed reference data where appropriate\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eproduce, maintain and update data models, pipelines and documentation for specific user, service and analytical needs\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emaintain metadata repositories, catalogues and governance arrangements for the data they create, transform and provision\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eapply quality checks, monitoring and controls across the data development lifecycle\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edesign data pipelines and platforms to be secure, resilient, scalable, sustainable and maintainable\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emaintain appropriate controls for AI-related data pipelines, including versioning, monitoring, reproducibility, auditability and safeguards against inappropriate or unauthorised use\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e"
      }

      "name": "8. Digital management practices",
      "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/government-functional-standard-govs-005-digital/government-functional-standard-govs-005-digital-html#digital-management-practices",
      "acceptedAnswer": {
        "@type": "Answer",
        "url": "https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/government-functional-standard-govs-005-digital/government-functional-standard-govs-005-digital-html#digital-management-practices",
        "text": "\u003ch3 id=\"overview-7\"\u003e8.1 Overview\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eThese practices support the development, delivery, operation and continuous improvement of sustainable government digital and data activity, including the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) where it is used in products, services or internal processes. They apply across the scope of this standard.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eManagers responsible for government digital and data activity, supported by subject matter experts where needed, should plan, manage and monitor work so that:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edelivery approaches are defined and assured (see 8.2)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003epolicy and business outcomes are met through user-centred, accessible and inclusive design (see 8.3)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003edigital components, data and AI-enabled systems are integrated or interoperable where appropriate (see 8.4)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eknowledge, information and data are managed appropriately (see 8.5)\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003echannels, user engagement, sustainability, assets, performance, reporting, capability, risk, procurement and contracts are managed effectively (see 8.6 to 8.12)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"delivery-approach\"\u003e8.2 Delivery approach\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"choose-the-right-delivery-approach\"\u003e8.2.1  Choose the right delivery approach\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eA delivery approach sets out how a solution is designed, delivered, implemented, operated, improved and decommissioned. For most government digital and data activity, the default should be agile, iterative and product-centred where appropriate, including where AI is being explored or used.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe person leading the work, such as a service owner, should define an approach that:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eassures quality, control and compliance with relevant standards and guidance\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eidentifies the skills, data, technology and supplier support needed\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econsiders specific assurance, security, ethical and human oversight requirements where AI is used\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe approach should reflect:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhether the work is new or an enhancement to an existing product or service\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econfidence in user needs, business requirements, data quality and technology choices\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etimescales, outputs, risks and whether value can be delivered incrementally\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eDifferent approaches may be used for different components of a wider system, provided they:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eintegrate at appropriate points\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emanage overall system risk\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ealign with government digital and data architecture, standards and patterns\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eAgile techniques, behaviours and incremental releases should be used where they deliver early user value, support learning and enable continuous improvement.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eServices (see section 5) shall be delivered in accordance with the Service Standard. \u003csup id=\"fnref:2:3\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:2\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 2]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"agile-delivery-approaches\"\u003e8.2.2 Agile delivery approaches\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eAgile delivery approaches are adaptive, iterative and incremental, and include:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebehaviours and culture\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emethods and techniques\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emanagement frameworks\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eAgile approaches should be used where rapid value creation, learning and flexibility are needed, and should normally be adopted for government digital and data activity unless a predictive approach is justified (see 8.2.3).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAgile culture and multi-disciplinary teams should support continuous improvement, delivery milestones and safe experimentation with emerging technologies, including AI.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGuidance about how to embed routine benchmarking of the organisation’s digital maturity should be followed.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSee Government Functional Standard GovS 002: Project Delivery.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"predictive-delivery-approaches\"\u003e8.2.3  Predictive delivery approaches\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere appropriate, a predictive delivery approach may be used instead of agile delivery.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePredictive approaches may be appropriate where incremental release is not feasible or would introduce unacceptable risk, for example:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003elarge capital infrastructure projects\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecomplex infrastructure remediation programmes\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etightly coupled legacy systems\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esafety-critical systems where test-and-learn would create substantial risk\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: Waterfall is a traditional software development approach and an example of a predictive, rather than iterative, approach. It is characterised by a sequential delivery where one step in delivery is completed before starting the next. Typically, this comprises: requirements, design, development, testing, and deployment.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"user-centred-design\"\u003e8.3 User-centred design\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eUser-centred design ensures digital products and services meet current and future user needs in an accessible, inclusive and timely way, while supporting policy and business outcomes. AI should be used where there is clear evidence that it meets user needs and improves outcomes.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: Attention is drawn to the public sector accessibility regulations. \u003csup id=\"fnref:11:2\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:11\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 11]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUser needs should be:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eidentified, understood and used to inform design and objectives\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ebalanced with policy, business, accessibility and inclusion outcomes\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esupported by transparency where AI affects data, decisions, outputs or user experience\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eUser needs should be used to design digital products and services that are simple, accessible, inclusive and efficient, enabling users to achieve their goals more easily than current practices allow.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: A user might be a member of the public, a person representing businesses or organisations, specific professionals, or anyone working within or for government (including third-party suppliers).\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"system-integration-and-interoperability\"\u003e8.4 System integration and interoperability\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eReusing technology, data, standards, patterns and common components, and designing for interoperability, reduces duplication, supports value for money and enables coherent user experiences. AI-enabled components should be designed to integrate safely and transparently with wider systems.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should develop and maintain catalogues for services, data, technology and reusable components where these are needed to support discovery, reuse, assurance and effective management.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eCatalogues should include public-facing and internal information, so that their content is discoverable and can be used or reused across the organisation and, where appropriate, by other government organisations.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"knowledge-and-information-management\"\u003e8.5 Knowledge and information management\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eKnowledge and information management ensures that knowledge, information and data are available, reliable and usable for delivery, assurance and decision making.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe organisation’s knowledge and information requirements should be understood and documented. Critical information and data should be identified in the organisation’s digital and data strategy, and reflected in the organisation’s plans (see 4.2.2) and asset management arrangements (see 8.8).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should define accountabilities for the ownership, protection, use, retention and disposal of information and data assets. This should include appropriate roles such as Information Asset Owners, Data Owners, Departmental Records Officers and the senior person accountable for information security risk, in line with organisational governance and relevant government guidance. Departmental Records Officers should help ensure compliance with records management and information management requirements, including the retention, disposal and transfer of official records.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe status, security classification, provenance, quality and permitted use of information and data should be clear, especially where data is used to train, test, operate or assure AI systems. Information should be retained to meet statutory, contractual and business requirements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGovernment Functional Standard GovS 007: Security shall be complied with, with respect to data and information security.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"use-of-channels-and-user-engagement\"\u003e8.6 Use of channels and user engagement\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eA channel is the medium to deliver information or a service to an end user.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eFor each service and across the service portfolio, organisations should understand:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003echannel usage, costs and transitions between channels\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhich channels are needed by different user groups\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow failures in one channel affect demand on others\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow services, including AI-assisted channels, remain accessible, inclusive and clear about when users are interacting with automation\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere user journeys are omnichannel, service owners should consider both usability and efficiency in their design.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eUsers’ feedback should be collected and managed. Where possible, users should be kept proactively informed of progress of the service, in order to reduce demand for updates.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA complaints procedure should be defined. Complaints should be resolved or explained in a timely way.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"sustainability\"\u003e8.7 Sustainability\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eDigital products and services should be designed, delivered and operated sustainably. This includes considering the environmental impact of technology choices, data storage, infrastructure and AI systems, as well as their resilience to climate risk.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSustainability requirements should be a key component of design, delivery and implementation as well as evaluation scores in procurement exercises. They should be included in the objectives and scope for the digital solution, and should be documented.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should adopt a circular and efficient approach to digital services and technology, by reusing common platforms, removing duplicate data and redundant services, and extracting value from end of life assets in life with the waste hierarchy.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe management of environment and sustainability should be covered in or referenced from a service’s defined delivery approach, if not already covered in organisation-wide policies and procedures. Relevant legislation shall be identified and must be complied with.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: See the Defra digital sustainability strategy 2025 to 2030 as an example departmental strategy for this topic.\u003csup id=\"fnref:38\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:38\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 38]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"configuration-and-asset-management\"\u003e8.8 Configuration and asset management\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"overview-8\"\u003e8.8.1  Overview\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eConfiguration management ensures that the assets needed to test and deliver a product or service are:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eworking consistently together\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003econtrolled in a consistent manner\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eaccurately and reliably documented\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esubject to two-way traceability\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThe approach to asset management should be included in digital and data strategies (see 4.2).\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAsset management plans should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esupport effective control across the government digital and data portfolio, including technology, data, models, AI components, tooling and legacy assets\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003einclude processes and frameworks to build stable and scalable systems\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003euse of configuration management tools\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003euse of common and interoperable tools across different projects and stages\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eThese plans should include expectations for future management of assets relating to legacy technology and services.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"manage-technology-assets\"\u003e8.8.2  Manage technology assets\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eTechnology assets should be managed throughout their life cycle to:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ereduce overall costs through retirement of redundant technology\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emanage technical debt\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003etrack technical alignment with other organisations\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eunderstand vendor usage and supply chain\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"manage-data-assets\"\u003e8.8.3 Manage data assets\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eData assets should be managed throughout the data life cycle so organisations understand what data they hold, where it is held, who can access it, how it is handled and whether it is suitable for reuse, analytics or AI. Organisations should maintain:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewhat data is held by the organisation\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ehow and where the data is held\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ewho has access to what data, in what circumstances\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethe handling arrangements for specific data\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eGuidance for data collection should be followed, including a controlled and consistent process for obtaining or importing data. Organisations should:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ekeep an original copy of data\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eback it up\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003emaintain metadata\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ekeep an audit trail\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eenable rollback where appropriate\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003eactively manage data quality.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eData should be retained only where necessary, and for the minimum period in line with legislation, retention policies and guidance or with the agreements in place with data owners.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eMetadata is information about the characteristics of the data, and how the data should be handled.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"performance-management\"\u003e8.9 Performance management\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should align with relevant cross-government performance frameworks to measure and report service performance, technology estate health, digital and data capability, organisational maturity and, where relevant, the performance and impact of AI-enabled systems.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"management-information-analytics-and-reporting\"\u003e8.10 Management information, analytics and reporting\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eManagement information should be accurate, complete and timely so people can undertake their roles and make informed decisions.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWorkflows, dashboards and standard reports should support monitoring, decision making and reporting. Where analytics or AI are used, outputs should be explainable, reliable and subject to appropriate human oversight.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eStandard, consistent reports should be available directly from the management information system to support internal and external activity, decision making and reporting.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eAppropriate data should be retained in accordance with the organisation’s data retention policy and prevailing legislation.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"digital-capacity-and-capability\"\u003e8.11 Digital capacity and capability\u003c/h3\u003e\u003cp\u003eDigital and data capacity and capability management balances supply and demand for skilled people, equipment, tooling, facilities and supplier support. This includes the capability needed to design, buy, use, assure and govern AI safely and effectively.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should maintain a view of current and future skills needs, address shortfalls, re-plan work where resources are constrained, and put business continuity measures in place for critical resources.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eWhere third parties provide better value, they should be used in line with relevant commercial, digital and data guidance, including the blueprint for modern digital government. \u003csup id=\"fnref:39\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:39\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 39]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations should capture third-party use and associated skills in capacity and capability plans.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eSenior civil servants within an organisation shall be assessed against the Digital and Data Essentials standard. \u003csup id=\"fnref:40\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:40\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 40]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGovernment Functional Standard GovS 003: People shall be complied with, with respect to people management.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch3 id=\"purchasing-and-contract-management\"\u003e8.12 Purchasing and contract management\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"procurement\"\u003e8.12.1  Procurement\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eOrganisations shall decide whether service solutions or components should be built internally, supplied by a third party, reused from existing government solutions, or delivered through a combination of approaches.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003ePurchasing strategies should support commercial, contractual, technology, data and AI considerations, including whether existing products or government solutions can meet the need.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eDecisions should take account of insights and research and should reflect that, where possible, commercial off-the-shelf products or existing solutions already in use across government should be used.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eBuilding or tailoring a solution should only be considered where:\u003c/p\u003e\u003cul\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003euser need is unique or rare\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003esupplier options are limited\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ecommercial products cannot be scaled, adapted or assured to meet the need\u003c/li\u003e\n  \u003cli\u003ethere are clear reasons to own, modify or control the technology, data or AI model\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003cp\u003eAn assessment of resources should be made to inform build or buy decisions, such as staff and funding, skills, operational capacity and the ability to deliver ongoing training.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGovernment Functional Standard GovS 008: Commercial shall be complied with, with respect to procurement and management of contracts.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eNote: See Should Cost modelling for purchasing strategy guidance. \u003csup id=\"fnref:41\"\u003e\u003ca href=\"#fn:41\" class=\"footnote\" rel=\"footnote\" role=\"doc-noteref\"\u003e[footnote 41]\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/sup\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003ch4 id=\"contract-management\"\u003e8.12.2  Contract management\u003c/h4\u003e\u003cp\u003eA contract management plan should define each party’s roles and responsibilities and be reviewed throughout the contract. For AI-enabled products or services, it should also cover transparency, security, data use, intellectual property, performance monitoring, assurance and exit arrangements.\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eGovernment Functional Standard GovS 008: Commercial shall be complied with.\u003c/p\u003e"
      }

        "text": "\u003cp\u003eSee also the \u003ca href=\"https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/functional-standards-common-glossary\"\u003ecommon glossary of definitions\u003c/a\u003e which includes a list of defined terms and phrases used across the suite of government standards. The glossary includes the term, definition, and which function owns the term and definition.\u003c/p\u003e\u003ctable\u003e\n  \u003cthead\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eTerm\u003c/th\u003e\n      \u003cth scope=\"col\"\u003eDefinition\u003c/th\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/thead\u003e\n  \u003ctbody\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003ealgorithmic transparency\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe practice of being open about where and how algorithmic tools are used, including their purpose, impact and governance.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eapplication programming interface (api)\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA set of rules and protocols that allows different software applications or systems to communicate with each other.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eartificial intelligence\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eTechnologies that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, prediction, classification or decision support.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eapplication (digital)\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA system for collecting, saving, processing, and presenting data by means of a computer. Note: The term application is generally used when referring to a component of software that can be executed.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003earchitecture (digital)\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eFundamental concepts or properties of a system in its environment embodied in its components, relationships, and in the principles of its design and evolution. Note: The term can be applied to any aspect of digital services, including service, data and technology.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003ecloud services\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eComputing services, such as storage, platforms, software or infrastructure, delivered over the internet and accessed on demand.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003ecatalogue\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eStructured information about aspects of a service or its components. Note: Examples include service catalogue (services offered or provided by a service provider), data catalogue, application catalogue, interface catalogue.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003echannel strategy (digital)\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA strategy to define the medium used to deliver a message to users of a service. Note: The channel can be a digital medium (such as a website or app), or a non-digital medium (such as a face-to-face appointment).\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003econfiguration item\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA component of a service or system that needs to be managed in order to deliver, maintain or support that service or system.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003edata\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eInformation that is collected, stored, processed, shared or used to support decisions, services and operations.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003edata quality\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe degree to which data is accurate, complete, timely, consistent and fit for its intended purpose.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003edata standard\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eAn agreed specification for how data is defined, structured, recorded, exchanged or managed.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003edigital\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eModern technology-enabled processes, business models, tools and ways of working.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003edigital asset\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eAnything that is stored digitally and is uniquely identifiable. Note: Digital assets can include data and technology assets.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003edigital product\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA software application that has one or more capabilities.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003edigital technology\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eDigital technologies are electronic tools, systems, devices and resources that generate, store or process data. They comprise both hardware and software components.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003edigital transformation\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe modernisation of technology, use of data, redesign of end-to-end processes, and more integrated ways of working to achieve improved services and business operations.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003edisaster recovery\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA set of defined activities related to how an organisation plans to recover from a disaster and return to a pre-disaster condition.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eevent (digital)\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA change of state that has significance for the management of a service or other configuration item.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eincident (digital)\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eIn the context of digital services, an incident is an unplanned   interruption to a service or reduction in the quality of a service.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003einteroperability\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe ability of systems, services, organisations or data to work together and exchange information effectively.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003elegacy (digital)\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA service or component part of a service which is no longer considered fit for purpose.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003elife cycle\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe stages through which a service, product, system, data asset or technology asset passes, from planning and design through delivery, operation, improvement and retirement.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eminimum viable product\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA service with just enough features to satisfy early users, and to provide feedback for future service development.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eomnichannel\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eDifferent channels integrated into a single user experience.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eopen standard\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA standard that is publicly available and can be used by anyone, supporting consistency, interoperability and reuse.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eproduct-centric delivery (digital)\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eProducts, capabilities and services that are delivered by a line of   business or multiple lines of business together, which are often grouped   around an end-to-end customer journey.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eproblem\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003ereference architecture\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA common structure, model or set of patterns that supports consistent design and implementation across related services, systems or data.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003erelease\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA version of a service or other configuration item, or a collection of configuration items, that is made available for use.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003ereliability\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe ability of a service or other configuration item to perform its intended function for a specified period of time or number of cycles under specified conditions.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eresilience (digital)\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe ability of an information system to continue to: (i) operate under adverse conditions or stress, even if in a degraded or debilitated state, while maintaining essential operational capabilities; and (ii) recover to an effective operational posture in a time frame consistent with mission needs.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eSource: Taken from The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eretirement\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003ePermanent withdrawal of a digital service or other configuration item from use.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003erisk management \u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe co-ordinated activities designed and operated to manage risk and exercise internal control within an organisation. \u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eroadmap\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA high-level plan that sets out the intended direction, outcomes, milestones and major activities needed to achieve an agreed strategy or objective.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003esecure by design\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe discipline of embedding cyber security into digital systems and services at every step of their life cycle - from the planning of a service, to the procurement and configuration of technology and retirement at end of life.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eservice\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA service captures all the things that collectively deliver an outcome   for users.     Note: A service is a complete solution that brings together technology and non-technology elements to enable users to achieve a defined   outcome.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eservice owner\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe person accountable for the overall quality, operation and continuous improvement of a service.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eservice backlog\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA list of new features, changes to existing features, bug fixes, infrastructure changes or other activities that a team may deliver in order to achieve a specific outcome. It is the single authoritative source for things that a service team works on.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eservice level\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eOne or more metrics that define expected or achieved service quality.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eservice level agreement\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eDocumented agreement between a service provider and users of a service that identifies the service provided and expected performance. Note: A service level agreement can be included in a contract or another type of documented agreement.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003esustainability\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe practice of designing, delivering and operating digital services and technology in a way that reduces environmental impact and supports long-term value.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003etechnical debt\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe implied cost of additional refactoring caused by choosing an expedient solution to deliver a piece of functionality or project instead of using an approach that would take longer or cost more.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eNote: This is typically calculated as the value of the hours required to refactor a piece of functionality or a project.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003etechnology code of practice\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA set of government guidance that helps organisations design, build and buy technology that is secure, sustainable, interoperable and aligned with user needs.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003etwo-way traceability\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eThe ability to trace both forward and backward (for example, from a   requirement to an element of the solution and from the solution element back   to the requirement).\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eNote: Two-way traceability can also be applied in other areas, such as to output-outcome-benefits mapping, and solution-plan mapping.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eNote: Two-way traceability is managed using configuration management.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003euser\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA person whose needs are to be met by a product, service   or process.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eNote: Users have a direct relationship with the product, service or process and might be end-users (such as a member of the public or a government official) or other users (such as those who maintain the product, service or process).\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003euser experience\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eHow a user interacts with and experiences a product, system, or service.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003euser-centred design\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA framework or process that focuses on putting users at the centre of   service or product design and development.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003euser journey\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eA sequence of events or experiences a user can   encounter while using a product or service.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003euser need\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003ePrerequisites identified as necessary for a user, or a set of users, to achieve an intended outcome, implied   or stated within a specific context of use.     Note: A user need is independent of any proposed solution for that need.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eNote: User needs are identified based on various approaches, including interviews with users,   observations, surveys, evaluations, expert analysis, etc.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eNote: User needs often represent gaps (or discrepancies) between what should be and what is.\u003cbr\u003e\u003cbr\u003eNote: User needs are transformed into user requirements by considering the context of use, user   priorities, trade-offs with other system requirements and constraints.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003evalidation\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eAn activity that ensures a solution (or part of) meets the needs of the   business. Validation ensures   that business requirements are met even though these might have changed   since the original design.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n    \u003ctr\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003everification\u003c/td\u003e\n      \u003ctd\u003eAn activity that ensures that a solution (or part of) is complete,   accurate, reliable and matches its design specification.\u003c/td\u003e\n    \u003c/tr\u003e\n  \u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e"
      }

        <div class="govspeak"><h2 id="purpose-and-scope">1.  Purpose and Scope</h2>

<h3 id="purpose-of-this-standard">1.1  Purpose of this standard</h3>

<p>This standard sets out what government organisations shall do to govern, deliver and assure digital and data activity. It helps organisations improve public services, work more efficiently and manage risk.</p>

<p>Organisations shall use a consistent approach so digital and data activity:</p>

<ul>
  <li>supports agreed policy and mission outcomes</li>
  <li>makes public services easier to access, use and improve</li>
  <li>improves productivity and efficiency across government</li>
  <li>supports services and platforms that work together, can scale and are resilient</li>
  <li>uses data to make decisions and improve continuously</li>
</ul>

<p>This standard is for:</p>

<ul>
  <li>senior accountable leaders, including permanent secretaries, directors general and chief executives of arm’s length bodies</li>
  <li>senior leaders accountable for digital and data, including chief digital and information officers and chief data officers</li>
  <li>senior leaders responsible for strategy, policy or service delivery</li>
  <li>practitioners who plan, deliver, operate or manage digital and data activity</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="scope-of-this-standard">1.2  Scope of this standard</h3>

<p>This standard applies to the whole lifecycle of government digital and data activity. This includes planning, designing, delivering, running and retiring:</p>

<ul>
  <li>public-facing and internal services</li>
  <li>technology and platforms</li>
  <li>data and data products</li>
</ul>

<p>This standard shall apply to government departments, arm’s length bodies and any other organisation in scope of a government functional standard.</p>

<p>GovS 005 addresses the governance, delivery, operation, resilience and lifecycle management of digital services, data and technology.</p>

<p>Cyber security requirements, controls and assurance expectations are set through GovS 007: Security.</p>

<p>Organisations should apply both standards together to ensure digital resilience and cyber security are managed coherently.</p>

<p>Other public sector organisations, including devolved administrations and local government, may adopt this standard or use it to support benchmarking and improvement.</p>

<h3 id="government-standards-references">1.3  Government standards references</h3>

<p>Organisations should use this standard with other relevant government functional standards set out on GOV UK. Each standard should be applied according to its own scope and accountabilities. <sup id="fnref:1"><a href="#fn:1" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 1]</a></sup></p>

<p>This standard is supported by The Service Standard <sup id="fnref:2"><a href="#fn:2" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 2]</a></sup>, which sets expectations for services, and the Technology Code of Practice <sup id="fnref:3"><a href="#fn:3" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 3]</a></sup>, which sets expectations for technology decisions.</p>

<p>The following Functional Standards are directly necessary for the use of this standard:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>GovS 002, Project delivery</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>GovS 003, Human resources</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>GovS 006, Finance</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>GovS 007, Security</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>GovS 008, Commercial</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>GovS 009, Internal audit</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>GovS 010, Analysis</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>GovS 013, Counter fraud</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>Together, these standards explain how government digital and data activity shall be governed, delivered, secured, measured and assured.</p>

<h2 id="principles">2.  Principles</h2>

<p>These principles set the expectations for how government digital and data activity should be planned, governed, delivered and improved to achieve user-centred, secure and measurable public outcomes.</p>

<p>They should provide clarity between organisational objectives, accountable delivery, proportionate assurance and continuous improvement across the full service and product lifecycle.</p>

<p>To strengthen their impact, the principles should be applied as strategic expectations, supported by evidence of ownership, risk management, performance, interoperability, data governance and ethical practice.</p>

<p>Anyone responsible for planning, developing, delivering or managing government digital and data activity shall ensure:</p>

<ol>
  <li>digital and data activity is aligned with government priorities, organisational objectives and the outcomes needed by users and the public</li>
  <li>governance, assurance and decision making are proportionate to the scale, stage and risk of the work</li>
  <li>accountability, ownership and responsibilities are clear across organisational and delivery boundaries</li>
</ol>

<p>4. services and products are designed around evidenced user needs, accessibility, inclusion and measurable outcomes</p>

<p>5. services, products and technology are managed throughout their lifecycle using evidence, feedback and performance data</p>

<p>6. technology and data are managed securely, lawfully and ethically, with appropriate controls for resilience, interoperability and reuse</p>

<p>7. teams have the skills, capacity and authority needed to deliver effectively and uphold public service values and professional standards</p>

<p>8. options and decisions are informed by a proportionate analysis of uncertainty, including risks, opportunities, assumptions and dependencies, taking into account the chances of different degrees of success or failure</p>

<p>9. government digital and data activity delivers value for money, in alignment with Managing Public Money, securing the appropriate combination of economy, efficiency and effectiveness needed to achieve the intended outcome</p>

<h2 id="context">3.  Context</h2>

<h3 id="introduction">3.1  Introduction</h3>

<p>This section explains the context for applying this functional standard. It sets out how government digital and data capabilities support policy outcomes, improve services, strengthen assurance, manage risk and help organisations work better.</p>

<h3 id="digital-transformation">3.2  Digital transformation</h3>

<p>Digital transformation means improving how government designs, delivers and manages services. Services should be simple, accessible, secure and efficient for users and organisations.</p>

<p>This includes improving whole services and processes, using data well, and making sure technology is secure, sustainable, interoperable and aligned to user and policy needs.</p>

<p>Effective delivery needs clear ownership across the lifecycle, multidisciplinary working and continuous improvement across services, technology and data. This means:</p>

<ul>
  <li>identifying accountable owners for services, products, technology and data across their lifecycle</li>
  <li>using multidisciplinary teams to work across organisational boundaries, improve outcomes, manage risk, measure performance and improve delivery</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="services">3.3  Services</h3>

<p>A service helps users achieve an outcome. It should reflect policy intent, legal requirements, operational needs and user needs.</p>

<p>Services can be public facing, such as applying for a licence, or internal, such as platforms that support finance, human resources or case management.</p>

<p>A service can include digital and non-digital parts that work together across the whole user journey. Digital parts can include online forms, notifications, application programming interfaces and casework tools. Non-digital parts can include assisted digital support, post, telephone contact and face-to-face interactions.</p>

<h3 id="technology">3.4  Technology</h3>

<p>Technology means the systems, platforms, infrastructure, applications and tools used to deliver, run, secure and improve government services and organisational capabilities.</p>

<p>This includes physical and cloud infrastructure, networks, end-user devices, hosting environments and other components used to create, process, store, secure and share information.</p>

<p>This includes artificial intelligence technologies. Organisations should select, buy, deploy and manage them safely, securely and responsibly, with clear lifecycle ownership, assurance, proportionate risk management and meaningful human control at the right stages.</p>

<p>Technology also includes software, applications, integrations, automation and code used to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>provide interfaces for users, staff and other systems</li>
  <li>support policy delivery, operational processes, service management and decision making</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="data">3.5  Data</h3>

<p>Data is information that government collects, creates, uses, shares and manages. It helps government understand needs, make decisions, deliver services, monitor performance, manage risk and improve outcomes.</p>

<p>Where data supports artificial intelligence tools, organisations should make sure it is lawful, relevant, accurate, secure and properly governed. They should identify and manage risks relating to privacy, fairness, bias, transparency and information quality.</p>

<p>Types of data include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>personal data, such as names, contact details and identifiers</li>
  <li>location and environmental data, such as geospatial reference data</li>
  <li>administrative and operational data about organisations, assets, services and transactions</li>
</ul>

<p>Uses for data include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>inform policy design, development, implementation and evaluation</li>
  <li>monitor and report on performance, outcomes, risk and value for money</li>
  <li>support service delivery and improvement, including eligibility checks, case management and service analytics</li>
  <li>help organisations understand performance, manage risk and make evidence-based decisions</li>
</ul>

<p>Organisations applying this standard should treat services, technology and data as connected parts of one delivery system. They should build clear ownership, proportionate assurance and continuous improvement into how they plan, deliver and manage outcomes.</p>

<h2 id="governance">4.  Governance</h2>

<h3 id="governance-and-management-framework">4.1  Governance and management framework</h3>

<h4 id="overview">4.1.1  Overview</h4>

<p>Governance covers prioritising, authorising, empowering, overseeing and assuring performance across government and within each organisation.</p>

<p>A governance and management framework shall be defined by those accountable for government digital and data activity. It should ensure governance is effective, proportionate, structured and aligned with cross-government priorities, including the safe, secure and responsible use of artificial intelligence.</p>

<p>It should include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>delegated authority limits, decision-making roles and rules, assurance needs, reporting structures, accountabilities and escalation routes</li>
  <li>management practices and documentation needed to meet this standard, including records of significant digital, data and AI-enabled systems where appropriate</li>
  <li>risk appetite and tolerance, risk ownership, reporting, oversight and escalation arrangements within the governance and management framework</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="governance-across-government">4.1.2  Governance across government</h4>

<p>A senior officer accountable for government digital and data strategy and planning across government shall be assigned (see 4.6.2). They should define the cross-government governance and management framework in consultation with organisational digital and data leaders (see 4.6.4).</p>

<p>The cross-government governance and management framework should include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>arrangements for developing and monitoring cross-government digital strategies and plans (see 4.2.1)</li>
  <li>cross-government service, technology and data standards</li>
  <li>capability requirements</li>
  <li>guidance for practitioners</li>
  <li>expectations for responsible AI adoption</li>
  <li>arrangements for identifying, assessing and managing systemic digital, data and technology risks</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="governance-within-each-organisation">4.1.3  Governance within each organisation</h4>

<p>Governance of government digital and data work within an organisation should be integrated with the organisation’s overall governance. The framework should bring together digital, data, service, technology, AI and wider business leaders so that work is prioritised, funded, delivered and improved in line with organisational objectives.</p>

<p>Each organisation’s governance and management framework should comply with:</p>

<ul>
  <li>government and departmental policies</li>
  <li>this functional standard and other relevant functional standards (see 1.2)</li>
  <li>cross-government standards and requirements (see 4.1.2)</li>
  <li>applicable AI guidance, ethics requirements, data protection obligations, security standards and assurance expectations</li>
  <li>statutory requirements</li>
</ul>

<p>As part of the governance and management framework, each organisation should develop and maintain:</p>

<ul>
  <li>required strategies and plans (see 4.2)</li>
  <li>a pipeline of proposed, current and completed work, including associated spend</li>
</ul>

<p>A senior officer accountable for the governance of the organisation’s government digital and data portfolio shall be assigned (see 4.6.4).</p>

<h3 id="strategy-and-planning">4.2  Strategy and planning</h3>

<h4 id="cross-government-digital-strategy">4.2.1  Cross-government digital strategy</h4>

<p>A cross-government strategy shall be developed and maintained to set the ambition for modern digital government and guide government digital and data work in organisations. It should reach at least three to five years into the future and set expectations for:</p>

<ul>
  <li>synergy, efficiency and interoperability of government digital and data activity, services, technology, data and related assets within and among organisations</li>
  <li>identifying and managing principal and systemic digital, data and technology risks, opportunities and dependencies across government</li>
  <li>significant programmes</li>
  <li>how organisational and government digital and data outcomes and targets will be achieved</li>
  <li>capability and capacity requirements</li>
  <li>how the strategy is to be implemented</li>
  <li>how AI and automation will be adopted responsibly to improve public services, productivity and decision support while maintaining public trust</li>
</ul>

<p>The cross-government digital and data strategy shall be developed in collaboration with senior business leaders and government digital and data specialists across government. It shall be communicated to organisations and used to support decision making (see 4.4).</p>

<p>Note: For current cross-government digital, data and AI expectations, see relevant government digital and data strategy, policy and guidance. <sup id="fnref:4"><a href="#fn:4" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 4]</a></sup></p>

<p>Note: For data and information, see the National Data Library. <sup id="fnref:5"><a href="#fn:5" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 5]</a></sup></p>

<h4 id="digital-strategy-and-planning-in-an-organisation">4.2.2 Digital strategy and planning in an organisation</h4>

<p>Each organisation should define and implement a government digital and data strategy, which shall:</p>

<ul>
  <li>align to the cross-government digital and data strategy (see 4.2.1)</li>
  <li>align to the organisation’s policy and strategy</li>
  <li>be subject to approval by the accounting officer (see 4.6.3)</li>
  <li>set out how AI will be used safely, lawfully, ethically and effectively, where relevant to organisational objectives</li>
</ul>

<p>The government digital and data strategy should be developed collaboratively by the organisation’s senior leaders and led by the senior officer accountable for the organisation’s government digital and data portfolio (see 4.6.4). It should reach at least three to five years into the future, and should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>outline the organisation’s ambition for how government digital and data capabilities will be used to achieve the organisation’s objectives</li>
  <li>include benchmarks which enable assessment of the organisation’s current performance and effectiveness</li>
  <li>outline plans for how the organisation will achieve its objectives for digital services, data, technology and capability</li>
  <li>describe the data, skills, governance and assurance needed to support responsible AI adoption</li>
</ul>

<p>The government digital and data strategy should be endorsed and actively supported by the accounting officer (see 4.6.3) and senior leadership, as this is critical to achieving effective digital transformation and better outcomes.</p>

<p>A detailed plan for government digital and data activity should set out owners, milestones, dependencies, risks and key performance indicators. Where AI is used, the plan should also define the intended benefits, data requirements, human oversight, assurance approach, model or tool ownership, monitoring arrangements and route for escalating risks. Plans should be agreed with relevant senior leaders and reviewed through governance and performance reporting.</p>

<h3 id="assurance">4.3  Assurance</h3>

<p>Assurance provides confidence to senior leaders and stakeholders that work is controlled, proportionate and supports successful delivery of policy, strategy and objectives.</p>

<p>Organisations should have a defined approach to assurance of government digital and data spend and activity. Assurance should be proportionate to risk, value and impact, integrated with the organisation’s overall assurance framework, and aligned to cross-government strategy, standards and expenditure controls.</p>

<p>AI-enabled activity should be assured across its lifecycle, including use case selection, data quality, privacy, security, ethical risk, bias, transparency, human oversight, procurement, operational monitoring and retirement. Assurance should confirm that AI is used only where it is appropriate, lawful, secure and supported by the right skills and controls.</p>

<p>Typically, assurance should be on at least three separate and defined levels, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>by, or on behalf of, the operational management team that owns and manages risk</li>
  <li>by, or on behalf of, senior management, independent of operational management, using specialist expertise to oversee management of the risk, and to ensure the first line of defence is properly designed and operating as intended</li>
  <li>by independent bodies to provide senior management with an objective opinion on the effectiveness of governance, risk management and internal controls, including the effectiveness of the previous lines of defence</li>
</ul>

<p>Recommendations provided through assurance processes should be incorporated into delivery planning at the earliest opportunity.</p>

<p>Note: Organisations should consider relevant cross-government assurance regimes, including GovAssure and related assurance requirements. <sup id="fnref:6"><a href="#fn:6" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 6]</a></sup></p>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 009: Internal Audit shall be complied with. <sup id="fnref:7"><a href="#fn:7" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 7]</a></sup></p>

<p>The requirements of the Orange Book: Management of Risk, Principles and Concepts, including Part II, the Risk Control Framework and its assurance expectations, shall be met. <sup id="fnref:8"><a href="#fn:8" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 8]</a></sup></p>

<h3 id="decision-making">4.4  Decision making</h3>

<p>Decisions relating to government digital and data activity should be made, approved and authorised in a timely way in accordance with the organisation’s governance and management framework. Where specified, minimum expectations shall be met (see 4.2.1).</p>

<p>Options and decisions should be based on clear criteria, evidence and user needs, and informed by a proportionate analysis of benefits and uncertainty, including risks, opportunities, assumptions and dependencies, taking into account the chances of different degrees of success or failure.</p>

<p>Key decisions relating to government digital and data activity should include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>alignment to cross-government and organisational strategy and plans</li>
  <li>authorising programmes and projects (see Government Functional Standard GovS 002: Project Delivery)</li>
  <li>efficiency and value</li>
  <li>sustainability of options, including the purchase of products and services (see Government Functional Standard GovS 008: Commercial)</li>
  <li>value for money, in alignment with Managing Public Money</li>
  <li>responsible use of AI, including lawfulness, ethics, data protection, transparency, explainability, human oversight, security, model performance and ongoing monitoring</li>
</ul>

<p>No organisation should make decisions which impact other organisations without having consulted them.</p>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 002: Project Delivery shall be complied with, with respect to portfolio, programme or project related decisions (such as initiating a project, authorising a new project phase, or responding to issues and risks).</p>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 008: Commercial shall be complied with, with respect to commercial decisions (such as deciding on a third-party supplier).</p>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 010: Analysis shall be complied with, with respect to the assessment of options.</p>

<p>Organisations shall comply with expenditure controls guidance. <sup id="fnref:9"><a href="#fn:9" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 9]</a></sup></p>

<p>Organisations shall comply with guidance on how to handle public funds. <sup id="fnref:10"><a href="#fn:10" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 10]</a></sup></p>

<h3 id="risk-management">4.5 Risk management</h3>

<p>Risk management supports informed decision making and helps digital products, services, data and technology operate successfully in support of objectives. It should address uncertainty, threats and opportunities, taking into account the chances of different degrees of success or failure. This includes risks arising from data, cyber security, legacy technology, third parties and AI.</p>
