<p>The senior officer accountable for the organisation’s digital portfolio (see 4.6.4) should ensure that management of risk is:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>integrated with the organisation’s overall risk management strategy</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>within the organisation’s risk appetite and tolerance</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>proportionate to the scale and complexity of the work</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>Risks associated with government digital and data activity should be represented at board level and reviewed regularly, including risks relating to sustainability of investment, continual improvement, capability, security, legacy technology, technical debt, data quality and AI use.</p>

<p>Digital resilience risks shall be owned, monitored and reported through organisational governance arrangements.</p>

<p>Organisational contingency and business continuity planning should be defined for services where failure presents a clear risk to organisational objectives. Accountability for enacting disaster recovery plans should be defined.</p>

<p>The requirements of the Orange Book: management of risk - principles and concepts, shall be met. <sup id="fnref:3:1"><a href="#fn:3" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 3]</a></sup></p>

<h3 id="roles-and-accountabilities">4.6  Roles and accountabilities</h3>

<h4 id="overview-1">4.6.1  Overview</h4>

<p>Roles and accountabilities shall be defined in governance and management frameworks and assigned to people with appropriate seniority, skills and experience.</p>

<p>This should include the activities, outputs or outcomes each role is responsible for, who they are accountable to, and how responsibilities are discharged for AI-enabled systems where relevant.</p>

<h4 id="senior-officer-accountable-for-digital-strategy-and-planning-across-government">4.6.2  Senior officer accountable for digital strategy and planning across government</h4>

<p>The senior officer accountable for government digital and data strategy and planning across government is accountable for:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>providing leadership and direction for government digital and data transformation and policy across government (see 3.2)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>collaborating within the organisation to identify, assess and manage systemic digital, data and technology risks, and supporting collective action to address common vulnerabilities, dependencies and capability gaps</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>setting and maintaining the cross-government governance and management framework (see 4.1)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>defining, communicating and implementing the cross-government digital and data strategy, policy and plans (see 4.2.1)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>continuous improvement in the government’s use of digital services, technology and data to support improved outcomes (see sections 5, 6, 7 and digital practices in section 8)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>setting expectations for responsible AI adoption across government, including governance, assurance, transparency, capability and risk management</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>Note: The Government Digital Service, part of the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, leads the Government Digital and Data function for government.</p>

<h4 id="accounting-officer">4.6.3  Accounting officer</h4>

<p>The permanent head of a government department is usually its principal accounting officer.</p>

<p>An organisation’s accounting officer is accountable (via a principal accounting officer where appropriate) to Parliament and the public for the stewardship of public resources, ensuring they are used effectively and to high standards of probity. The principal accounting officer generally appoints the most senior executive in the arm’s length bodies within the department’s ambit as an accounting officer.</p>

<p>The accounting officer is accountable for ensuring the organisation’s government digital and data strategy is appropriate (see 4.2.2), and should create an environment in which their organisation:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>endorses and actively supports government digital and data transformation</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>plans and manages government digital and data activity in accordance with this standard</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>uses AI responsibly and proportionately, with appropriate governance, assurance, transparency and human oversight</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<h4 id="senior-officer-accountable-for-an-organisations-digital-portfolio">4.6.4  Senior officer accountable for an organisation’s digital portfolio</h4>

<p>The senior officer accountable for an organisation’s government digital and data portfolio is accountable to the accounting officer for:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>providing leadership and direction for government digital and data transformation within the organisation</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>ensuring government and organisational policies are complied with</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>setting and maintaining the organisation’s governance and management framework (see 4.1)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>setting, communicating and implementing the organisation’s government digital and data strategy and plans (see 4.2)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>ensuring continuous improvement of government digital and data activity is a priority within the organisation</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>supporting integrated management of digital and non-digital aspects of services, working with the senior officer accountable for service delivery (see 4.6.7)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>managing government digital and data risk within the organisation’s risk appetite and tolerance (see 4.5)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>ensuring AI-related risks are identified, owned, assured and managed within the organisation’s risk appetite and legal obligations</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>collaborating within the organisation to identify, assess and manage systemic digital, data and technology risks, and supporting collective action to address common vulnerabilities, dependencies and capability gaps</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>The senior officer accountable for an organisation’s government digital and data portfolio should be a member of the organisation’s senior decision-making forums to ensure that government digital and data priorities, risks and dependencies are represented.</p>

<p>Note: In the majority of organisations this role is, but not limited to, a Director or Director General.</p>

<p>Note: This role is often known as Chief Digital Officer or Chief Digital and Information Officer and would usually lead the organisation’s Government Digital and Data function.</p>

<p>Note: See Government Functional Standard GovS 002: Project Delivery for more on portfolio, programme or project management.</p>

<h4 id="senior-officer-accountable-for-data-in-an-organisation">4.6.5  Senior officer accountable for data in an organisation</h4>

<p>The senior officer accountable for data in an organisation is accountable to the senior officer accountable for the organisation’s government digital and data portfolio (see 4.6.4), for managing the organisation’s data and information assets, including data and information used to support AI-enabled systems, in relation to government digital and data activity.</p>

<p>The senior officer accountable for data is responsible for ensuring that the organisation:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>adopts and complies with relevant data, information governance and security requirements (see 4.1)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>develops, maintains and implements a data and information strategy and plan (see 4.2)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>assigns roles and responsibilities for the ownership, stewardship and management of data and information assets, including accountability for quality, access, retention, protection, reuse and remediation of issues</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>is enabled to use data and information to drive improvement in its productivity and services</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>ensures data and information used for AI-enabled systems is suitable, lawful, secure, well-governed, appropriately documented and monitored for quality, provenance, bias, performance impact and drift</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>In large, complex organisations, where use of data relates to discrete business areas with different legal or security requirements, accountability for managing a subset of the organisation’s data may be separately delegated. In these cases, the data and information strategy and plan should explain how relevant interfaces are defined and managed.</p>

<p>See section 7, Data management.</p>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 007: Security shall be complied with, with respect to data and information security. In line with this, organisations should consider appointing a data protection specialist role.</p>

<p>Note: This role is often known as the Chief Data Officer.</p>

<p>Note: This role might also be accountable to the senior officer accountable for analysis in an organisation for analysis related activity. See Government Functional Standard GovS 010: Analysis.</p>

<h4 id="senior-officer-accountable-for-technology-in-an-organisation">4.6.6  Senior officer accountable for technology in an organisation</h4>

<p>The senior officer accountable for government digital and data in an organisation is accountable to the senior officer accountable for the organisation’s government digital and data portfolio (see 4.6.4), for managing the organisation’s government digital and data solutions (see section 6), and for ensuring that the organisation:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>adopts and complies with relevant government digital and data requirements and guidance (see 4.1)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>develops, maintains and implements a government digital and data strategy and plan (see 4.2)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>assigns appropriate roles and responsibilities for the ownership and management of government digital and data solutions</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>has an appropriate approach to technical security and resilience</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>ensures AI-enabled solutions are designed, procured, implemented and monitored in line with security, resilience, ethics, assurance and data protection requirements</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>This role should provide technical direction for the design and delivery of services (see section 5), ensuring that government digital and data solutions, including AI-enabled solutions, are appropriate, cost-effective, scalable, secure, resilient and operationally sustainable.</p>

<p>See section 6, Government digital and data management.</p>

<p>Note: This role is often known as the Chief Technology Officer. In large or complex organisations, it is often supported by a Chief Architect.</p>

<h4 id="senior-officer-accountable-for-service-delivery">4.6.7  Senior officer accountable for service delivery</h4>

<p>The senior officer accountable for service delivery is accountable to the accounting officer for directing the integrated management of the organisation’s service delivery operations, ensuring that:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>the portfolio of services, including digital and non-digital elements, meets policy and organisational objectives</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>the organisation uses performance data and user feedback to understand how well services are performing in terms of usability and efficiency</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>AI or automation used in service delivery is transparent, monitored, explainable where appropriate, and subject to meaningful human oversight for significant decisions</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>accountabilities and responsibilities for each service are assigned, with service owners taking end-to-end responsibility (see 4.6.8)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>appropriate provision is made for users who are not using digital channels</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>Where an organisation’s portfolio of services is complex or very large, accountability for a sub-portfolio of services may be delegated (directly by the accounting officer, or from this role), provided the resulting user and product interfaces are defined and managed.</p>

<p>Note: In a government department or large arm’s length body, with services comprising a mix of digital and non-digital components, it is likely that a Director General or Chief Operating Officer would be the appropriate person to undertake this role.</p>

<h4 id="service-owner">4.6.8  Service owner</h4>

<p>The service owner is accountable to the senior officer accountable for service delivery (4.6.7) for the oversight and promotion of their assigned end-to-end service (see section 5), including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>developing and operating the service holistically (covering digital and any non-digital elements) to meet user needs, operate efficiently, and maintain required levels of performance (see 8.9)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>maintaining a service backlog to support the setting of priorities for continuous improvements, enhancements and updates</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>ensuring necessary approval processes are followed, and risks and issues are mitigated (see 4.5)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>ensuring AI-enabled service changes are tested, monitored and assured before and after deployment</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>securing and managing costs and pricing, where appropriate</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>managing customer relations and responding to user feedback (see 8.6)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>service transition and retirement, where necessary</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<p>The service owner is accountable for ensuring that relevant roles and responsibilities for delivery of the service are assigned and documented, and for the integrated management of the service across the multi-disciplinary delivery team.</p>

<p>The service owner should be supported by a digital service manager (see 4.6.9) to manage the specific digital aspects of the service. Where appropriate and justified, this role may be combined with the role of digital service manager to streamline operations, for example where a service is delivered only through digital channels.</p>

<h4 id="digital-service-manager">4.6.9  Digital service manager</h4>

<p>The digital service manager is responsible for the development and day-to-day operation of the digital aspects of their assigned service (see section 5), and is accountable to the service owner for:</p>

<ul>
  <li>
    <p>ensuring the digital service meets user needs (see 8.3)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>managing digital content and design</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>planning, tracking, reviewing and reporting on the operation of the digital service (see 5.4)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>ensuring there is useful and timely performance and management information data (see 5.6) on the services, and that this is consistent with cross-government standards</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>prioritising and managing workflow</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>responding to and resolving problems, incidents and issues</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>escalating risks and issues as needed (see 4.5)</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>delivering continuous improvements, enhancements and updates</p>
  </li>
  <li>
    <p>ensuring any AI-assisted operational activity is appropriately monitored, reviewed and escalated where risks, inaccuracies or service impacts arise</p>
  </li>
</ul>

<h2 id="service-management">5. Service management</h2>

<h3 id="overview-2">5.1  Overview</h3>

<p>This section provides a framework for developing, managing, improving and, where needed, retiring services.</p>

<p>Services should be digital where this best meets user needs, and should be developed and delivered by multi-disciplinary teams using agile methods.</p>

<p>Accountability for the ownership and management of service delivery and each service shall be assigned (see 4.6.7 and 4.6.8).</p>

<h3 id="policy-intent">5.2  Policy intent</h3>

<p>Policy intent should be reflected in the organisation’s business strategy, business plan and service portfolio (see 5.5).</p>

<p>Service outcomes, efficiencies and benefits should be defined and traceable to the achievement of, or support for, policy intent.</p>

<p>Policy owners and those accountable for service delivery should work in cross-functional teams under a single service owner, so policy intent is reflected continuously.</p>

<h3 id="service-design-and-development">5.3  Service design and development</h3>

<p>New, changed or transformed services should provide value to government and users, and be usable and efficient. See GovS 002, Project delivery.</p>

<p>Services shall be delivered in accordance with the Service Standard. <sup id="fnref:2:1"><a href="#fn:2" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 2]</a></sup></p>

<p>User research (see 8.3), iterative development and, where appropriate, testing of AI-enabled components should continue throughout the service life cycle.</p>

<p>Services shall be monitored using consistent service performance measures (see 5.6), reviewed quarterly.</p>

<p>Where services are not digital, or perform poorly against usability and efficiency measures, the service owner should consider redesigning the service end-to-end.</p>

<p>Organisations buying off-the-shelf products, services or AI-enabled tools should ensure suppliers can meet user needs and relevant standards. See 6.3 and GovS 008, Commercial.</p>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 007: Security shall be complied with by embedding cyber security into digital services, including any AI-enabled components, throughout the life cycle.</p>

<p>Note: Advice and guidance about technology choices can be found in the Technology Code of Practice. <sup id="fnref:3:2"><a href="#fn:3" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 3]</a></sup></p>

<p>Note: Where AI is used in a service, it should be used only where there is clear evidence of user need, with appropriate human oversight, assurance, transparency, security and monitoring.</p>

<p>Note: The Service Manual includes advice on creating and running public services that meet the Service Standard. <sup id="fnref:11"><a href="#fn:11" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 11]</a></sup></p>

<h3 id="service-management-1">5.4  Service management</h3>

<p>Services should be documented so their architecture, components and connections are defined and understood. This should include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>user-facing and internal systems</li>
  <li>the people and the tasks they carry out to run the service</li>
  <li>processes</li>
  <li>data flows, decision points and any AI-enabled components</li>
</ul>

<p>A target operating model should be developed and maintained for each service. It should set out the delivery approach (see 8.2), working practices and processes, people and skills, and the data, technology and AI capabilities needed to provide the service in line with government digital and data ways of working.</p>

<p>Integrated management should cover:</p>

<ul>
  <li>digital and non-digital components of a service</li>
  <li>the service and the wider system of systems of which it is part, including dependencies on other organisations that provide parts of the same user journey</li>
</ul>

<p>Services should be delivered and improved iteratively to meet changing user needs, developments in technology, including AI where appropriate, and changes in government policy, releasing value through frequent deployment cycles.</p>

<p>Service owners and teams should use qualitative and quantitative evidence, including performance analytics (see 5.6), user feedback, user research (see 8.3) and evidence from AI monitoring where relevant, to prioritise iterative delivery and improvement. Improvements should be managed through a single service backlog.</p>

<h3 id="management-of-the-organisations-portfolio-of-services">5.5  Management of the organisation’s portfolio of services</h3>

<p>Organisations should maintain a service catalogue so public-facing and internal services, technologies and AI-enabled capabilities are discoverable for use and possible reuse across the organisation and by other organisations.</p>

<p>The portfolio of services should be maintained to ensure:</p>

<ul>
  <li>technology, data, AI-enabled and non-digital components are planned and managed as a unified and consistent system</li>
  <li>there is a consistent portfolio-wide view of material risks, opportunities, concentrations of risk, inter-service dependencies and systemic vulnerabilities, with clear ownership and escalation arrangements</li>
  <li>user journeys across multiple services are streamlined and deliver a consistent user experience</li>
  <li>there is a consistent view of performance and prioritisation, as well as dependencies between services</li>
  <li>feedback informs future design and delivery across the organisation’s services</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="performance-metrics-and-feedback">5.6  Performance metrics and feedback</h3>

<p>The service owner should define and collect performance metrics, taking account of the cross-government performance framework and any additional assurance needed for AI-enabled components.</p>

<p>Service performance targets should be established, managed and aligned with cross-government performance metrics. They should include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>data on usability and efficiency of the service</li>
  <li>meeting defined service levels</li>
  <li>accuracy, reliability, bias, transparency and human oversight measures where AI is used</li>
</ul>

<p>Performance against targets should be reported to senior leaders and stakeholders, and should meet requirements in the cross-government governance and management framework (see 4.1).</p>

<h3 id="accessible-and-inclusive-services">5.7  Accessible and inclusive services</h3>

<p>Accessible and inclusive services ensure any potential user can use the service regardless of their personal characteristics, situation, capabilities or access needs, and has equal access and opportunity.</p>

<p>Digital services shall be designed and managed to meet defined user abilities and accessibility requirements. Relevant legislation shall be identified and must be complied with, including where AI affects access, decisions, content or user support.</p>

<p>Those accountable for service development and delivery should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>build services that are intuitive to use, and present complicated information as simply as possible</li>
  <li>consider and address the barriers different groups of users might face when trying to use the service</li>
  <li>encourage users to use digital services, while providing help, human support and non-digital alternatives for those without the skills or access to use the digital option</li>
  <li>make sure users know which channels are available to them</li>
</ul>

<p>Note: Guidance on making services inclusive can be found in the Service Manual. <sup id="fnref:11:1"><a href="#fn:11" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 11]</a></sup></p>

<p>Note: The Service Standard sets requirements for accessibility, usability, consistency and efficiency. <sup id="fnref:2:2"><a href="#fn:2" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 2]</a></sup></p>

<p>Note: Attention is drawn to the public sector accessibility regulations. <sup id="fnref:12"><a href="#fn:12" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 12]</a></sup></p>

<h3 id="service-retirement">5.8  Service retirement</h3>

<p>The senior officer accountable for the organisation’s service delivery (see 4.6.7) may decide to retire a service, taking advice from the service owner. This might reflect changes in policy or user need, consolidation with another service, or replacement of legacy technology, including AI-enabled components where relevant.</p>

<p>Once the decision to retire a service has been taken, the service owner should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>archive or move relevant assets</li>
  <li>inform and support the public or business users to migrate to any new service</li>
  <li>consider dependencies across and beyond the organisation’s service portfolio, including data, technology and AI dependencies</li>
  <li>ensure impacted stakeholders are engaged</li>
  <li>review and, where needed, decommission AI models, prompts, data pipelines and monitoring arrangements safely</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="technology-management">6.  Technology management</h2>

<h3 id="overview-3">6.1  Overview</h3>

<p>A senior officer accountable for government digital and data shall be assigned in each organisation (see 4.6.6).</p>

<p>The senior officer should ensure insights, research, data, technology and emerging capabilities, including artificial intelligence (AI), inform the organisation’s strategy, architecture and asset management approach (see 8.8).</p>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 002: Project Delivery shall be complied with, with respect to work that is part of a portfolio, programme or project.</p>

<p>AI should be considered as part of the wider government digital and data landscape where it supports user needs, public value, operational effectiveness or better decision-making. Any use of AI should be lawful, ethical, secure, transparent and subject to appropriate human oversight, assurance and risk management.</p>

<p>Relevant strategy, policy and subject specific standards should be followed, including:</p>

<ul>
  <li>The Technology Code of Practice <sup id="fnref:3:3"><a href="#fn:3" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 3]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Cloud First Strategy <sup id="fnref:13"><a href="#fn:13" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 13]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Managing Vendor Lock-in <sup id="fnref:14"><a href="#fn:14" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 14]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>National Institute of Standards and Technology <sup id="fnref:15"><a href="#fn:15" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 15]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Cyber Essentials <sup id="fnref:16"><a href="#fn:16" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 16]</a></sup>
</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="technology-development-and-maintenance">6.2  Technology development and maintenance</h3>

<p>Digital and data architecture sets the parameters for the configuration, interaction and interdependence of the components, services, data assets and systems that enable government digital and data solutions.</p>

<p>Architecture should align with the relevant target operating model, service needs and data requirements (see 5.4 and 8.4).</p>

<p>Digital and data architecture should reflect the organisation’s government digital and data strategy, support current and future service delivery, and remain deliverable within the organisation’s risk appetite (see 4.5).</p>

<p>In keeping with the published standards (see 6.1), government digital and data solutions should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>be secure by design</li>
  <li>use open standards and open code</li>
  <li>adhere to relevant classification standards</li>
  <li>protect data at rest and in transit</li>
  <li>include appropriate governance, assurance and lifecycle controls where AI capabilities are used</li>
</ul>

<p>Government digital and data products, services and systems should be understood and actively managed. Governance controls should reduce legacy technology, manage technical debt, track cross-government alignment, understand supplier and supply-chain dependencies, and avoid unnecessary duplication. Controls should also cover business continuity, resilience and, where AI is used, model performance, data quality, bias, security, transparency, accountability and ongoing assurance.</p>

<p>Organisations should identify, document and manage risks and dependencies, including external dependencies and supply chains, especially where shared services, shared data arrangements or AI-enabled capabilities are in place (see 4.5).</p>

<p>Government digital and data solutions may be developed and managed in-house, by third-party suppliers, or through a combination of both. Where AI components are procured, built or integrated, roles, responsibilities, assurance requirements and supplier obligations should be defined from the outset (see 4.5).</p>

<h3 id="deployment-and-operation-of-technology">6.3  Deployment and operation of technology</h3>

<h4 id="overview-4">6.3.1  Overview</h4>

<p>Each organisation should have mechanisms for managing and continually improving its government digital and data solutions, so that changing business, policy, operational and user needs continue to be met.</p>

<p>Relevant roles and responsibilities should be defined and assigned to reflect the organisation’s build or buy choices, including responsibility for AI-enabled components where applicable (see 4.5).</p>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 007: Security shall be complied with, with respect to a mechanism being in place for identifying and resolving security vulnerabilities.</p>

<p>Note: For buy (third-party delivery), responsibilities are defined in the contract; for build (in-house delivery) see Technology Code of Practice guidance. <sup id="fnref:3:4"><a href="#fn:3" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 3]</a></sup></p>

<h4 id="operations-management">6.3.2  Operations management</h4>

<p>The senior officer accountable for government digital and data (see 4.6.6) should ensure those managing digital and data solutions have the capability, capacity and defined processes to run, operate and continuously improve them.</p>

<p>Processes should be defined and managed, and responsibility assigned for:</p>

<ul>
  <li>ensuring clean, secure and maintainable code for the organisation</li>
  <li>maintaining, iterating, and patching solutions against known vulnerabilities</li>
  <li>understanding, identifying and remediating potential risks, with effective operational monitoring, including relevant service management processes such as incident management, problem management and disaster recovery</li>
  <li>ensuring consistent and tested business continuity arrangements are in place and understood by all stakeholders</li>
  <li>monitoring AI-enabled components where used, including performance, drift, data quality, security risks, explainability, human oversight and escalation routes</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="triggers-for-change">6.3.3  Triggers for change</h4>

<p>Triggers for change should be understood and managed. They are likely to relate to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>internally generated change derived from operating digital and data solutions, including user feedback, data insights and performance metrics</li>
  <li>externally generated change derived from a new or updated policy, a public announcement, supplier expiry or another external reason</li>
  <li>change generated from decisions taken about the organisation’s digital and data architecture (see 6.2)</li>
  <li>changes in AI capability, regulation, risk profile, model performance, data quality or assurance requirements</li>
</ul>

<p>Addressing triggers for change might result in incremental change, service improvement, technical remediation, or upgrades managed through a project or programme.</p>

<p>The organisation’s legacy technology, data stores, digital services and AI-enabled components should be defined and monitored. An up-to-date plan should be maintained to remediate, replace or retire them.</p>

<p>Technology, data stores, digital services or AI-enabled components become legacy when they meet any of the following conditions:</p>

<ul>
  <li>considered an end-of-life product</li>
  <li>out of support or on extended support from the supplier</li>
  <li>impossible to update</li>
  <li>no longer cost-effective</li>
  <li>considered to be above the acceptable risk threshold</li>
  <li>no longer meet required levels of assurance, explainability, data quality, security or human oversight</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="retirement-of-government-digital-and-data-solutions">6.4  Retirement of government digital and data solutions</h3>

<h4 id="overview-5">6.4.1  Overview</h4>

<p>The purpose of retirement is to ensure government digital and data solutions remain fit for purpose. A solution should be considered for retirement if:</p>

<ul>
  <li>it is not possible to update or improve the existing solution to meet future business, policy, operational or user needs</li>
  <li>there are resource constraints</li>
  <li>the solution represents poor value for money</li>
  <li>there is a reduction or ending of future supplier support</li>
  <li>identified risks are unacceptably high</li>
  <li>it is incompatible with the ambition set by the organisation’s government digital and data strategy</li>
  <li>AI-enabled components can no longer be assured, monitored, explained, secured or controlled to an acceptable standard</li>
</ul>

<p>The senior officer accountable for government digital and data in an organisation (see 4.6.6) should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>identify components, systems, data stores or services that are no longer capable of meeting the organisation’s needs</li>
  <li>identify the services or business operations that rely on the solution intended for retirement</li>
  <li>consult service owners, data owners and other stakeholders that rely on the existing solution, to understand their priorities for future operation</li>
  <li>assess whether any AI-enabled components, models, training data, prompts, outputs, logs or derived data need to be retained, migrated, archived or deleted</li>
  <li>oversee service delivery teams to ensure the management and retirement of the solution and, where necessary, its replacement, meets the organisation’s needs</li>
  <li>work with service owners and stakeholders to ensure all data is migrated, archived or removed in line with data protection, classification and information assurance requirements</li>
  <li>lead the removal and appropriate disposal of retired technology, systems and data assets</li>
</ul>

<p>Necessary replacement arrangements should be in place before retirement takes place.</p>

<p>Note: Retire includes withdrawal from existing services or operations, and disposal of associated technology, systems, data assets and AI-enabled components.</p>

<h4 id="withdraw-technology">6.4.2  Withdraw technology</h4>

<p>The process and complexity of moving away from legacy systems, data stores, technologies and AI-enabled components varies depending on the solution involved.</p>

<p>Note: For example, decommissioning physical hardware such as laptops is more straightforward than decommissioning a mainframe and building a replacement system in the cloud.</p>

<p>Before a solution is withdrawn, the following actions should be taken:</p>

<ul>
  <li>review existing contractual arrangements and take any necessary action to end the contract, if appropriate</li>
  <li>prepare data that is to be migrated</li>
  <li>plan transition of services to alternative solutions, if required</li>
  <li>define and implement a secure process for migrating data between systems, or data removal and destruction based on the information assurance needs and any GDPR data associated with the system</li>
  <li>confirm whether any AI models, configuration, prompts, outputs, logs, training data or evaluation records need to be retained, transferred, archived or securely destroyed</li>
  <li>engage with staff and other users affected by the change, and provide necessary training or guidance</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="dispose-of-technology-systems-and-data-assets">6.4.3  Dispose of technology, systems and data assets</h4>

<p>The service owner (see 4.6.8) and the senior officer accountable for government digital and data in an organisation (see 4.6.6) should ensure redundant equipment, systems, data assets and AI-enabled components are appropriately disposed of.</p>

<p>Disposal shall meet security requirements, and any physical hardware disposal should, where possible, be recycled using recognised and sustainable approaches.</p>

<p>When decommissioning cloud-based assets or AI-enabled services, processes should ensure residual data, models, logs, outputs and configuration are not accessible post-disposal. Relevant security guidance should always be considered when disposing of technology.</p>

<p>Requirements for the handling of personal data being moved or removed must be followed in accordance with prevailing regulations and security advice, including where personal data has been used in AI-enabled systems.</p>

<p>Note: Attention is drawn to the following requirements:</p>

<ul>
  <li>UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) <sup id="fnref:17"><a href="#fn:17" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 17]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>The Data Protection Act <sup id="fnref:18"><a href="#fn:18" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 18]</a></sup>
</li>
</ul>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 007: Security shall be complied with when disposing of technology, systems, data assets and AI-enabled components.</p>

<p>Where AI-enabled components are retired or disposed of, organisations should ensure models, prompts, outputs, logs, training data, evaluation records and configuration are handled in line with data protection, security, information assurance and retention requirements.</p>

<h2 id="data-management">7. Data management</h2>

<h3 id="overview-6">7.1 Overview</h3>

<p>This section sets expectations for managing data as a strategic asset that supports better public services, evidence-based decisions, operational effectiveness and responsible innovation across government, including the safe and transparent use of artificial intelligence.</p>

<p>Each organisation shall assign senior accountability for data, with clear ownership for data strategy, governance, quality, protection, ethical use, sharing and reuse (see 4.6.5).</p>

<p>Organisations should follow cross-government strategies, standards and governance for government digital and data, including guidance from the Data Standards Authority, the Government Data Quality Framework, the Data and AI Ethics Framework, the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard, and relevant security, privacy and technology standards (see section 4).</p>

<p>Data should be retained, archived or disposed of in accordance with the organisation’s retention schedule, information management policy, security requirements and legislation.</p>

<p>Note: The National Data Library is the home of UK public data to inform decisions and build services. <sup id="fnref:5:1"><a href="#fn:5" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 5]</a></sup></p>

<p>Note: Attention is drawn to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) <sup id="fnref:17:1"><a href="#fn:17" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 17]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>The Data Protection Act <sup id="fnref:18:1"><a href="#fn:18" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 18]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Public Records Act <sup id="fnref:19"><a href="#fn:19" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 19]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Freedom of Information Act <sup id="fnref:20"><a href="#fn:20" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 20]</a></sup>
</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="data-management-principles">7.2 Data management principles</h3>

<p>Data management must be lawful, ethical, secure, transparent and proportionate to the purpose for which data is collected, used, shared and retained.</p>

<p>Organisations should ensure their data is fit for purpose by:</p>

<ul>
  <li>identifying critical data assets, including those needed for service delivery, policy, operations, analysis, reporting, cross-government sharing and AI-enabled services</li>
  <li>assigning accountable owners and stewards for critical data assets, with clear responsibilities for governance, quality, access, protection and lifecycle management</li>
  <li>maintaining metadata and catalogues so that data can be found, understood, validated, reused and shared appropriately</li>
  <li>putting processes in place to identify, prioritise, remediate and monitor data quality issues at source</li>
</ul>

<p>Organisations should ensure their data is trusted, accessible and reusable by:</p>

<ul>
  <li>being able to evidence that critical data assets meet minimum standards for governance, quality, security, privacy and ethical use, based on their purpose and context</li>
  <li>ensuring data is discoverable through maintained catalogues, with clear metadata, lineage, quality information and access conditions</li>
  <li>applying appropriate security, privacy, access and information assurance controls so data can be shared safely and lawfully</li>
</ul>

<p>Organisations should ensure their data architecture (see 7.4) supports interoperability, reuse and secure exchange by:</p>

<ul>
  <li>identifying authoritative sources for critical data and ensuring they are appropriately governed, maintained and provisioned</li>
  <li>using open standards, common data models and agreed reference data where appropriate to improve consistency and interoperability</li>
  <li>being able to evidence that Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), data exchange platforms and analytical environments meet appropriate standards for governance, security, privacy and control</li>
  <li>documenting classifications, sensitivity, criticality, retention requirements, lineage and usage restrictions so data is handled appropriately</li>
  <li>maintaining integrated catalogues for data, interfaces, standards and data sharing arrangements</li>
  <li>ensuring data used to train, test, validate or operate AI systems is documented, lawful, representative, secure and appropriate for the intended use</li>
</ul>

<p>There should be accountable ownership for data quality, protection, security, ethics, access, sharing and reuse, supported by cross-government guidance, frameworks and standards.</p>

<p>To support continuous improvement and help senior leaders prioritise investment, organisations should assess data maturity across technical, governance, cultural, skills and leadership factors using an appropriate framework.</p>

<p>Throughout the planning, implementation and evaluation of projects, programmes, services, analytical work and AI-enabled solutions, organisations should use the Data and AI Ethics Framework to ensure data and AI are used appropriately, responsibly and transparently. <sup id="fnref:21"><a href="#fn:21" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 21]</a></sup></p>

<p>See Government Functional Standard GovS 002: Project Delivery.</p>

<p>Where specified, publication of data and analysis should be done through approved routes.</p>

<p>For example, publication of official statistics should follow the protocols set out in the Code of Practice for Statistics, which provides the framework for trustworthy, high-quality and valuable statistics. These principles are relevant across data management and should be followed where appropriate. <sup id="fnref:22"><a href="#fn:22" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 22]</a></sup></p>

<p>Note: The Data Standards Authority exists to improve how the public sector manages data, including by setting standards for sharing and using data across government. <sup id="fnref:23"><a href="#fn:23" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 23]</a></sup></p>

<p>Note: The government’s Data and AI Ethics Framework guides appropriate and responsible use of data, data-driven technologies, automated decision-making and AI in government and the wider public sector.</p>

<p>It helps public servants identify ethical considerations, manage risks and maintain trust across the lifecycle of data and AI projects.</p>

<h3 id="data-frameworks-and-operating-models">7.3 Data frameworks and operating models</h3>

<p>Organisations shall follow appropriate guidance when implementing data frameworks and operating models, including for cross-government data sharing, business intelligence, artificial intelligence, machine learning, automation and advanced analytics.</p>

<p>Note: The following products provide best practice guidance:</p>

<ul>
  <li>Principles for securing personal data in government services <sup id="fnref:24"><a href="#fn:24" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 24]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>AI Playbook for UK Government <sup id="fnref:25"><a href="#fn:25" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 25]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Data and AI Ethics Framework <sup id="fnref:21:1"><a href="#fn:21" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 21]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard <sup id="fnref:26"><a href="#fn:26" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 26]</a></sup>
</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="data-architecture">7.4 Data architecture</h3>

<p>Data architecture describes the systems, processes, standards, models and structures used to acquire, create, move, store, query, protect, share, archive and dispose of data to meet user, service and business needs.</p>

<p>Organisations need confidence that the right data is available when needed, in usable, accessible, secure and standardised formats, and that data and system capabilities meet user, service and operational needs.</p>

<p>When developing data architecture proposals, organisations should follow relevant standards, guidance and tools, including open standards, API standards, security guidance, data protection requirements, AI assurance guidance and guidance on managing data assets (see 8.8).</p>

<p>Note: For practical advice, see the data management capability framework and the GOV.UK collection of design guidance for application programming interfaces. <sup id="fnref:27"><a href="#fn:27" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 27]</a></sup></p>

<p>The following web-based API standards guidance will help your organisation deliver the best possible services to users:</p>

<ul>
  <li>UK Government Reference Architecture for Data and APIs <sup id="fnref:28"><a href="#fn:28" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 28]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>GraphQL Guidance - an API specification originally developed by Facebook as an alternative to REST for querying complex data structures <sup id="fnref:29"><a href="#fn:29" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 29]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>API Management Guidance - enabling you to standardise how teams design, launch and manage APIs in your organisation <sup id="fnref:30"><a href="#fn:30" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 30]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Domain Guidance for api.gov.uk - contact the Government Digital Service to get a domain for your API on GOV.UK <sup id="fnref:31"><a href="#fn:31" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 31]</a></sup>
</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="managing-data-quality">7.4.1  Managing data quality</h4>

<p>Data quality should be measured using dimensions such as completeness, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness, validity and accuracy. The dimensions and thresholds used should reflect the intended use, risk, sensitivity and impact of the data, including where data supports AI or automated decision-making.</p>

<p>Organisations should develop a culture of data quality, by:</p>

<ul>
  <li>treating issues at source and committing to ongoing monitoring, reporting and continuous improvement</li>
  <li>targeting improvements where they add the most value or reduce the greatest risk</li>
  <li>managing data quality proactively across the data lifecycle</li>
  <li>making data quality visible to users through metadata, quality statements or other appropriate information</li>
</ul>

<p>A data quality action plan may be used to manage improvement work. If used, it should identify owners, priorities, root causes, actions, measures, timescales and reporting arrangements, and should be reflected in the organisation’s information and data plan (see 8.5).</p>

<p>Organisations should use measurable characteristics to improve data quality, and should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>maintain an assessment of the current level of data quality</li>
  <li>set targets for appropriate quality levels in the future</li>
  <li>monitor quality to ensure that planned improvements are made</li>
</ul>

<p>Such quality measures should ensure that accountability is clear (see 4.6.5) and that:</p>

<ul>
  <li>quality characteristics are assessed in relation to a specific use at various points</li>
  <li>the impact of changes to relevant data collection, storage, and processing is assessed</li>
</ul>

<p>Note: The Data Quality Hub provides information and support on data quality. <sup id="fnref:32"><a href="#fn:32" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 32]</a></sup></p>

<p>Note: Further information and guidance can be found in the Data Quality Framework. <sup id="fnref:33"><a href="#fn:33" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 33]</a></sup></p>

<h3 id="data-and-information-asset-management">7.5 Data and information asset management</h3>

<p>Data and information asset management enables an organisation to identify, record, understand, govern and maintain its data and information assets so it knows what it holds, where it is held, who is accountable for it, how it can be accessed, how it should be protected, and how it is retained, reused, shared or disposed of.</p>

<p>Organisations should follow existing standards and guidance, including the data asset management policy where applicable, and should manage data so that:</p>

<ul>
  <li>critical data and information assets are identified, recorded, maintained and reported where required</li>
  <li>metadata is actively managed to describe data and information assets, ownership, quality, lineage, sensitivity, retention, disposal and access conditions</li>
  <li>data is shared by default where lawful, ethical, secure and appropriate, and where there are no valid reasons not to share</li>
  <li>data is reused to maximise value and minimise unnecessary duplication, collection and storage</li>
  <li>dataset linkage is managed safely, with appropriate privacy, security and ethical controls</li>
  <li>access permissions are strictly managed and reviewed regularly</li>
  <li>data governance, security, privacy and compliance requirements are observed throughout the data lifecycle</li>
  <li>interoperable data infrastructure, open standards and integrated catalogues are used where appropriate</li>
  <li>data assets used in AI systems are recorded with their purpose, provenance, quality, limitations, access conditions and retention requirements</li>
</ul>

<p>Note: For information asset ownership, see government guidance on the Information Asset Owner role. <sup id="fnref:34"><a href="#fn:34" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 34]</a></sup></p>

<p>Note: The resources listed provide best practice for managing and supporting data asset management:</p>

<ul>
  <li>API Catalogue <sup id="fnref:35"><a href="#fn:35" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 35]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Reference Data for Use Across Government <sup id="fnref:36"><a href="#fn:36" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 36]</a></sup>
</li>
  <li>Address Base Guidance - use free property and street information to add geospatial data to your projects and comply with the UPRN standard <sup id="fnref:37"><a href="#fn:37" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 37]</a></sup>
</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="data-engineering">7.6 Data engineering</h3>

<p>The purpose of data engineering is to make data useful, accessible, reliable and secure for authorised users so they can make informed decisions, improve services and optimise organisational performance.</p>

<p>Data engineering includes acquiring, ingesting, validating, transforming, modelling, documenting, storing, securing and provisioning data in formats that meet user needs and support safe reuse, including for analytics, automation and AI where appropriate.</p>

<p>To ensure useful and accessible data through data engineering, organisations should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>follow cross-government data standards, open standards and agreed reference data where appropriate</li>
  <li>produce, maintain and update data models, pipelines and documentation for specific user, service and analytical needs</li>
  <li>maintain metadata repositories, catalogues and governance arrangements for the data they create, transform and provision</li>
  <li>apply quality checks, monitoring and controls across the data development lifecycle</li>
  <li>design data pipelines and platforms to be secure, resilient, scalable, sustainable and maintainable</li>
  <li>maintain appropriate controls for AI-related data pipelines, including versioning, monitoring, reproducibility, auditability and safeguards against inappropriate or unauthorised use</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="digital-management-practices">8. Digital management practices</h2>

<h3 id="overview-7">8.1 Overview</h3>

<p>These practices support the development, delivery, operation and continuous improvement of sustainable government digital and data activity, including the responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) where it is used in products, services or internal processes. They apply across the scope of this standard.</p>

<p>Managers responsible for government digital and data activity, supported by subject matter experts where needed, should plan, manage and monitor work so that:</p>

<ul>
  <li>delivery approaches are defined and assured (see 8.2)</li>
  <li>policy and business outcomes are met through user-centred, accessible and inclusive design (see 8.3)</li>
  <li>digital components, data and AI-enabled systems are integrated or interoperable where appropriate (see 8.4)</li>
  <li>knowledge, information and data are managed appropriately (see 8.5)</li>
  <li>channels, user engagement, sustainability, assets, performance, reporting, capability, risk, procurement and contracts are managed effectively (see 8.6 to 8.12)</li>
</ul>

<h3 id="delivery-approach">8.2 Delivery approach</h3>

<h4 id="choose-the-right-delivery-approach">8.2.1  Choose the right delivery approach</h4>

<p>A delivery approach sets out how a solution is designed, delivered, implemented, operated, improved and decommissioned. For most government digital and data activity, the default should be agile, iterative and product-centred where appropriate, including where AI is being explored or used.</p>

<p>The person leading the work, such as a service owner, should define an approach that:</p>

<ul>
  <li>assures quality, control and compliance with relevant standards and guidance</li>
  <li>identifies the skills, data, technology and supplier support needed</li>
  <li>considers specific assurance, security, ethical and human oversight requirements where AI is used</li>
</ul>

<p>The approach should reflect:</p>

<ul>
  <li>whether the work is new or an enhancement to an existing product or service</li>
  <li>confidence in user needs, business requirements, data quality and technology choices</li>
  <li>timescales, outputs, risks and whether value can be delivered incrementally</li>
</ul>

<p>Different approaches may be used for different components of a wider system, provided they:</p>

<ul>
  <li>integrate at appropriate points</li>
  <li>manage overall system risk</li>
  <li>align with government digital and data architecture, standards and patterns</li>
</ul>

<p>Agile techniques, behaviours and incremental releases should be used where they deliver early user value, support learning and enable continuous improvement.</p>

<p>Services (see section 5) shall be delivered in accordance with the Service Standard. <sup id="fnref:2:3"><a href="#fn:2" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 2]</a></sup></p>

<h4 id="agile-delivery-approaches">8.2.2 Agile delivery approaches</h4>

<p>Agile delivery approaches are adaptive, iterative and incremental, and include:</p>

<ul>
  <li>behaviours and culture</li>
  <li>methods and techniques</li>
  <li>management frameworks</li>
</ul>

<p>Agile approaches should be used where rapid value creation, learning and flexibility are needed, and should normally be adopted for government digital and data activity unless a predictive approach is justified (see 8.2.3).</p>

<p>Agile culture and multi-disciplinary teams should support continuous improvement, delivery milestones and safe experimentation with emerging technologies, including AI.</p>

<p>Guidance about how to embed routine benchmarking of the organisation’s digital maturity should be followed.</p>

<p>See Government Functional Standard GovS 002: Project Delivery.</p>

<h4 id="predictive-delivery-approaches">8.2.3  Predictive delivery approaches</h4>

<p>Where appropriate, a predictive delivery approach may be used instead of agile delivery.</p>

<p>Predictive approaches may be appropriate where incremental release is not feasible or would introduce unacceptable risk, for example:</p>

<ul>
  <li>large capital infrastructure projects</li>
  <li>complex infrastructure remediation programmes</li>
  <li>tightly coupled legacy systems</li>
  <li>safety-critical systems where test-and-learn would create substantial risk</li>
</ul>

<p>Note: Waterfall is a traditional software development approach and an example of a predictive, rather than iterative, approach. It is characterised by a sequential delivery where one step in delivery is completed before starting the next. Typically, this comprises: requirements, design, development, testing, and deployment.</p>

<h3 id="user-centred-design">8.3 User-centred design</h3>

<p>User-centred design ensures digital products and services meet current and future user needs in an accessible, inclusive and timely way, while supporting policy and business outcomes. AI should be used where there is clear evidence that it meets user needs and improves outcomes.</p>

<p>Note: Attention is drawn to the public sector accessibility regulations. <sup id="fnref:11:2"><a href="#fn:11" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 11]</a></sup></p>

<p>User needs should be:</p>

<ul>
  <li>identified, understood and used to inform design and objectives</li>
  <li>balanced with policy, business, accessibility and inclusion outcomes</li>
  <li>supported by transparency where AI affects data, decisions, outputs or user experience</li>
</ul>

<p>User needs should be used to design digital products and services that are simple, accessible, inclusive and efficient, enabling users to achieve their goals more easily than current practices allow.</p>

<p>Note: A user might be a member of the public, a person representing businesses or organisations, specific professionals, or anyone working within or for government (including third-party suppliers).</p>

<h3 id="system-integration-and-interoperability">8.4 System integration and interoperability</h3>

<p>Reusing technology, data, standards, patterns and common components, and designing for interoperability, reduces duplication, supports value for money and enables coherent user experiences. AI-enabled components should be designed to integrate safely and transparently with wider systems.</p>

<p>Organisations should develop and maintain catalogues for services, data, technology and reusable components where these are needed to support discovery, reuse, assurance and effective management.</p>

<p>Catalogues should include public-facing and internal information, so that their content is discoverable and can be used or reused across the organisation and, where appropriate, by other government organisations.</p>

<h3 id="knowledge-and-information-management">8.5 Knowledge and information management</h3>

<p>Knowledge and information management ensures that knowledge, information and data are available, reliable and usable for delivery, assurance and decision making.</p>

<p>The organisation’s knowledge and information requirements should be understood and documented. Critical information and data should be identified in the organisation’s digital and data strategy, and reflected in the organisation’s plans (see 4.2.2) and asset management arrangements (see 8.8).</p>

<p>Organisations should define accountabilities for the ownership, protection, use, retention and disposal of information and data assets. This should include appropriate roles such as Information Asset Owners, Data Owners, Departmental Records Officers and the senior person accountable for information security risk, in line with organisational governance and relevant government guidance. Departmental Records Officers should help ensure compliance with records management and information management requirements, including the retention, disposal and transfer of official records.</p>

<p>The status, security classification, provenance, quality and permitted use of information and data should be clear, especially where data is used to train, test, operate or assure AI systems. Information should be retained to meet statutory, contractual and business requirements.</p>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 007: Security shall be complied with, with respect to data and information security.</p>

<h3 id="use-of-channels-and-user-engagement">8.6 Use of channels and user engagement</h3>

<p>A channel is the medium to deliver information or a service to an end user.</p>

<p>For each service and across the service portfolio, organisations should understand:</p>

<ul>
  <li>channel usage, costs and transitions between channels</li>
  <li>which channels are needed by different user groups</li>
  <li>how failures in one channel affect demand on others</li>
  <li>how services, including AI-assisted channels, remain accessible, inclusive and clear about when users are interacting with automation</li>
</ul>

<p>Where user journeys are omnichannel, service owners should consider both usability and efficiency in their design.</p>

<p>Users’ feedback should be collected and managed. Where possible, users should be kept proactively informed of progress of the service, in order to reduce demand for updates.</p>

<p>A complaints procedure should be defined. Complaints should be resolved or explained in a timely way.</p>

<h3 id="sustainability">8.7 Sustainability</h3>

<p>Digital products and services should be designed, delivered and operated sustainably. This includes considering the environmental impact of technology choices, data storage, infrastructure and AI systems, as well as their resilience to climate risk.</p>

<p>Sustainability requirements should be a key component of design, delivery and implementation as well as evaluation scores in procurement exercises. They should be included in the objectives and scope for the digital solution, and should be documented.</p>

<p>Organisations should adopt a circular and efficient approach to digital services and technology, by reusing common platforms, removing duplicate data and redundant services, and extracting value from end of life assets in life with the waste hierarchy.</p>

<p>The management of environment and sustainability should be covered in or referenced from a service’s defined delivery approach, if not already covered in organisation-wide policies and procedures. Relevant legislation shall be identified and must be complied with.</p>

<p>Note: See the Defra digital sustainability strategy 2025 to 2030 as an example departmental strategy for this topic.<sup id="fnref:38"><a href="#fn:38" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 38]</a></sup></p>

<h3 id="configuration-and-asset-management">8.8 Configuration and asset management</h3>

<h4 id="overview-8">8.8.1  Overview</h4>

<p>Configuration management ensures that the assets needed to test and deliver a product or service are:</p>

<ul>
  <li>working consistently together</li>
  <li>controlled in a consistent manner</li>
  <li>accurately and reliably documented</li>
  <li>subject to two-way traceability</li>
</ul>

<p>The approach to asset management should be included in digital and data strategies (see 4.2).</p>

<p>Asset management plans should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>support effective control across the government digital and data portfolio, including technology, data, models, AI components, tooling and legacy assets</li>
  <li>include processes and frameworks to build stable and scalable systems</li>
  <li>use of configuration management tools</li>
  <li>use of common and interoperable tools across different projects and stages</li>
</ul>

<p>These plans should include expectations for future management of assets relating to legacy technology and services.</p>

<h4 id="manage-technology-assets">8.8.2  Manage technology assets</h4>

<p>Technology assets should be managed throughout their life cycle to:</p>

<ul>
  <li>reduce overall costs through retirement of redundant technology</li>
  <li>manage technical debt</li>
  <li>track technical alignment with other organisations</li>
  <li>understand vendor usage and supply chain</li>
</ul>

<h4 id="manage-data-assets">8.8.3 Manage data assets</h4>

<p>Data assets should be managed throughout the data life cycle so organisations understand what data they hold, where it is held, who can access it, how it is handled and whether it is suitable for reuse, analytics or AI. Organisations should maintain:</p>

<ul>
  <li>what data is held by the organisation</li>
  <li>how and where the data is held</li>
  <li>who has access to what data, in what circumstances</li>
  <li>the handling arrangements for specific data</li>
</ul>

<p>Guidance for data collection should be followed, including a controlled and consistent process for obtaining or importing data. Organisations should:</p>

<ul>
  <li>keep an original copy of data</li>
  <li>back it up</li>
  <li>maintain metadata</li>
  <li>keep an audit trail</li>
  <li>enable rollback where appropriate</li>
  <li>actively manage data quality.</li>
</ul>

<p>Data should be retained only where necessary, and for the minimum period in line with legislation, retention policies and guidance or with the agreements in place with data owners.</p>

<p>Metadata is information about the characteristics of the data, and how the data should be handled.</p>

<h3 id="performance-management">8.9 Performance management</h3>

<p>Organisations should align with relevant cross-government performance frameworks to measure and report service performance, technology estate health, digital and data capability, organisational maturity and, where relevant, the performance and impact of AI-enabled systems.</p>

<h3 id="management-information-analytics-and-reporting">8.10 Management information, analytics and reporting</h3>

<p>Management information should be accurate, complete and timely so people can undertake their roles and make informed decisions.</p>

<p>Workflows, dashboards and standard reports should support monitoring, decision making and reporting. Where analytics or AI are used, outputs should be explainable, reliable and subject to appropriate human oversight.</p>

<p>Standard, consistent reports should be available directly from the management information system to support internal and external activity, decision making and reporting.</p>

<p>Appropriate data should be retained in accordance with the organisation’s data retention policy and prevailing legislation.</p>

<h3 id="digital-capacity-and-capability">8.11 Digital capacity and capability</h3>

<p>Digital and data capacity and capability management balances supply and demand for skilled people, equipment, tooling, facilities and supplier support. This includes the capability needed to design, buy, use, assure and govern AI safely and effectively.</p>

<p>Organisations should maintain a view of current and future skills needs, address shortfalls, re-plan work where resources are constrained, and put business continuity measures in place for critical resources.</p>

<p>Where third parties provide better value, they should be used in line with relevant commercial, digital and data guidance, including the blueprint for modern digital government. <sup id="fnref:39"><a href="#fn:39" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 39]</a></sup></p>

<p>Organisations should capture third-party use and associated skills in capacity and capability plans.</p>

<p>Senior civil servants within an organisation shall be assessed against the Digital and Data Essentials standard. <sup id="fnref:40"><a href="#fn:40" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 40]</a></sup></p>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 003: People shall be complied with, with respect to people management.</p>

<h3 id="purchasing-and-contract-management">8.12 Purchasing and contract management</h3>

<h4 id="procurement">8.12.1  Procurement</h4>

<p>Organisations shall decide whether service solutions or components should be built internally, supplied by a third party, reused from existing government solutions, or delivered through a combination of approaches.</p>

<p>Purchasing strategies should support commercial, contractual, technology, data and AI considerations, including whether existing products or government solutions can meet the need.</p>

<p>Decisions should take account of insights and research and should reflect that, where possible, commercial off-the-shelf products or existing solutions already in use across government should be used.</p>

<p>Building or tailoring a solution should only be considered where:</p>

<ul>
  <li>user need is unique or rare</li>
  <li>supplier options are limited</li>
  <li>commercial products cannot be scaled, adapted or assured to meet the need</li>
  <li>there are clear reasons to own, modify or control the technology, data or AI model</li>
</ul>

<p>An assessment of resources should be made to inform build or buy decisions, such as staff and funding, skills, operational capacity and the ability to deliver ongoing training.</p>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 008: Commercial shall be complied with, with respect to procurement and management of contracts.</p>

<p>Note: See Should Cost modelling for purchasing strategy guidance. <sup id="fnref:41"><a href="#fn:41" class="footnote" rel="footnote" role="doc-noteref">[footnote 41]</a></sup></p>

<h4 id="contract-management">8.12.2  Contract management</h4>

<p>A contract management plan should define each party’s roles and responsibilities and be reviewed throughout the contract. For AI-enabled products or services, it should also cover transparency, security, data use, intellectual property, performance monitoring, assurance and exit arrangements.</p>

<p>Government Functional Standard GovS 008: Commercial shall be complied with.</p>

<h2 id="glossary">Glossary</h2>

<p>See also the <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/functional-standards-common-glossary">common glossary of definitions</a> which includes a list of defined terms and phrases used across the suite of government standards. The glossary includes the term, definition, and which function owns the term and definition.</p>
