      <th scope="col">Term</th>
      <th scope="col">Definition</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>algorithmic transparency</td>
      <td>The practice of being open about where and how algorithmic tools are used, including their purpose, impact and governance.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>application programming interface (api)</td>
      <td>A set of rules and protocols that allows different software applications or systems to communicate with each other.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>artificial intelligence</td>
      <td>Technologies that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, prediction, classification or decision support.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>application (digital)</td>
      <td>A system for collecting, saving, processing, and presenting data by means of a computer. Note: The term application is generally used when referring to a component of software that can be executed.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>architecture (digital)</td>
      <td>Fundamental concepts or properties of a system in its environment embodied in its components, relationships, and in the principles of its design and evolution. Note: The term can be applied to any aspect of digital services, including service, data and technology.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>cloud services</td>
      <td>Computing services, such as storage, platforms, software or infrastructure, delivered over the internet and accessed on demand.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>catalogue</td>
      <td>Structured information about aspects of a service or its components. Note: Examples include service catalogue (services offered or provided by a service provider), data catalogue, application catalogue, interface catalogue.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>channel strategy (digital)</td>
      <td>A strategy to define the medium used to deliver a message to users of a service. Note: The channel can be a digital medium (such as a website or app), or a non-digital medium (such as a face-to-face appointment).</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>configuration item</td>
      <td>A component of a service or system that needs to be managed in order to deliver, maintain or support that service or system.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>data</td>
      <td>Information that is collected, stored, processed, shared or used to support decisions, services and operations.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>data quality</td>
      <td>The degree to which data is accurate, complete, timely, consistent and fit for its intended purpose.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>data standard</td>
      <td>An agreed specification for how data is defined, structured, recorded, exchanged or managed.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>digital</td>
      <td>Modern technology-enabled processes, business models, tools and ways of working.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>digital asset</td>
      <td>Anything that is stored digitally and is uniquely identifiable. Note: Digital assets can include data and technology assets.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>digital product</td>
      <td>A software application that has one or more capabilities.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>digital technology</td>
      <td>Digital technologies are electronic tools, systems, devices and resources that generate, store or process data. They comprise both hardware and software components.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>digital transformation</td>
      <td>The modernisation of technology, use of data, redesign of end-to-end processes, and more integrated ways of working to achieve improved services and business operations.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>disaster recovery</td>
      <td>A set of defined activities related to how an organisation plans to recover from a disaster and return to a pre-disaster condition.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>event (digital)</td>
      <td>A change of state that has significance for the management of a service or other configuration item.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>incident (digital)</td>
      <td>In the context of digital services, an incident is an unplanned   interruption to a service or reduction in the quality of a service.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>interoperability</td>
      <td>The ability of systems, services, organisations or data to work together and exchange information effectively.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>legacy (digital)</td>
      <td>A service or component part of a service which is no longer considered fit for purpose.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>life cycle</td>
      <td>The stages through which a service, product, system, data asset or technology asset passes, from planning and design through delivery, operation, improvement and retirement.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>minimum viable product</td>
      <td>A service with just enough features to satisfy early users, and to provide feedback for future service development.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>omnichannel</td>
      <td>Different channels integrated into a single user experience.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>open standard</td>
      <td>A standard that is publicly available and can be used by anyone, supporting consistency, interoperability and reuse.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>product-centric delivery (digital)</td>
      <td>Products, capabilities and services that are delivered by a line of   business or multiple lines of business together, which are often grouped   around an end-to-end customer journey.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>problem</td>
      <td>A cause, or potential cause, of one or more incidents.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>reference architecture</td>
      <td>A common structure, model or set of patterns that supports consistent design and implementation across related services, systems or data.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>release</td>
      <td>A version of a service or other configuration item, or a collection of configuration items, that is made available for use.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>reliability</td>
      <td>The ability of a service or other configuration item to perform its intended function for a specified period of time or number of cycles under specified conditions.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>resilience (digital)</td>
      <td>The ability of an information system to continue to: (i) operate under adverse conditions or stress, even if in a degraded or debilitated state, while maintaining essential operational capabilities; and (ii) recover to an effective operational posture in a time frame consistent with mission needs.<br><br>Source: Taken from The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>retirement</td>
      <td>Permanent withdrawal of a digital service or other configuration item from use.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>risk management </td>
      <td>The co-ordinated activities designed and operated to manage risk and exercise internal control within an organisation. </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>roadmap</td>
      <td>A high-level plan that sets out the intended direction, outcomes, milestones and major activities needed to achieve an agreed strategy or objective.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>secure by design</td>
      <td>The discipline of embedding cyber security into digital systems and services at every step of their life cycle - from the planning of a service, to the procurement and configuration of technology and retirement at end of life.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>service</td>
      <td>A service captures all the things that collectively deliver an outcome   for users.     Note: A service is a complete solution that brings together technology and non-technology elements to enable users to achieve a defined   outcome.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>service owner</td>
      <td>The person accountable for the overall quality, operation and continuous improvement of a service.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>service backlog</td>
      <td>A list of new features, changes to existing features, bug fixes, infrastructure changes or other activities that a team may deliver in order to achieve a specific outcome. It is the single authoritative source for things that a service team works on.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>service level</td>
      <td>One or more metrics that define expected or achieved service quality.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>service level agreement</td>
      <td>Documented agreement between a service provider and users of a service that identifies the service provided and expected performance. Note: A service level agreement can be included in a contract or another type of documented agreement.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>sustainability</td>
      <td>The practice of designing, delivering and operating digital services and technology in a way that reduces environmental impact and supports long-term value.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>technical debt</td>
      <td>The implied cost of additional refactoring caused by choosing an expedient solution to deliver a piece of functionality or project instead of using an approach that would take longer or cost more.<br><br>Note: This is typically calculated as the value of the hours required to refactor a piece of functionality or a project.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>technology code of practice</td>
      <td>A set of government guidance that helps organisations design, build and buy technology that is secure, sustainable, interoperable and aligned with user needs.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>two-way traceability</td>
      <td>The ability to trace both forward and backward (for example, from a   requirement to an element of the solution and from the solution element back   to the requirement).<br><br>Note: Two-way traceability can also be applied in other areas, such as to output-outcome-benefits mapping, and solution-plan mapping.<br><br>Note: Two-way traceability is managed using configuration management.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>user</td>
      <td>A person whose needs are to be met by a product, service   or process.<br><br>Note: Users have a direct relationship with the product, service or process and might be end-users (such as a member of the public or a government official) or other users (such as those who maintain the product, service or process).</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>user experience</td>
      <td>How a user interacts with and experiences a product, system, or service.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>user-centred design</td>
      <td>A framework or process that focuses on putting users at the centre of   service or product design and development.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>user journey</td>
      <td>A sequence of events or experiences a user can   encounter while using a product or service.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>user need</td>
      <td>Prerequisites identified as necessary for a user, or a set of users, to achieve an intended outcome, implied   or stated within a specific context of use.     Note: A user need is independent of any proposed solution for that need.<br><br>Note: User needs are identified based on various approaches, including interviews with users,   observations, surveys, evaluations, expert analysis, etc.<br><br>Note: User needs often represent gaps (or discrepancies) between what should be and what is.<br><br>Note: User needs are transformed into user requirements by considering the context of use, user   priorities, trade-offs with other system requirements and constraints.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>validation</td>
      <td>An activity that ensures a solution (or part of) meets the needs of the   business. Validation ensures   that business requirements are met even though these might have changed   since the original design.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>verification</td>
      <td>An activity that ensures that a solution (or part of) is complete,   accurate, reliable and matches its design specification.</td>
    </tr>
